And so the proofs ran over into the third day. This very thing was now fine and old-fashioned: that the Senate should be broken off by night, summoned for three days, held for three days.
11.19. Cornutus Tertullus, consul-elect, an excellent man and most firm for the truth, moved that the seven hundred thousand sesterces which Marius had received be paid into the treasury, that Marius be forbidden Rome and Italy, and Marcianus this further, Africa as well. At the end of his motion he added that, since I and Tacitus had diligently and bravely performed the advocacy enjoined upon us, the Senate judged that we had acted in a manner worthy of the parts entrusted to us.

title: Letters
text:
11.20. The consuls-elect assented, and all the consulars too, down to Pompeius Collega: he moved that the seven hundred thousand be paid into the treasury, that Marcianus be banished for five years, but that Marius be left to the penalty for extortion which he had already suffered.
11.21. There were many on each side, perhaps even more on this, the looser and milder, opinion. For some even of those who seemed to have assented to Cornutus were following the one who had moved after them.
11.22. But when the division came, those who had stood by the consuls' chairs began to go over to Cornutus's opinion. Then those who had let themselves be counted with Collega crossed to the other side; Collega was left with a few. He afterwards complained much of those who had urged him on, especially of Regulus, who had deserted him in the opinion he had himself dictated. And Regulus has, moreover, so unstable a temper that he dares the most and fears the most.
11.23. This was the end of a most weighty inquiry. Yet there remains a little business, by no means slight: Hostilius Firminus, legate of Marius Priscus, who, being mixed up in the case, was gravely and vehemently harassed. For it was proved, both by Marcianus's accounts and by a speech which he himself had made before the council of the people of Lepcis, that he had lent his aid to Priscus for a most disgraceful service, and had stipulated for fifty thousand denarii from Marcianus; and that he had besides received ten thousand sesterces under a most foul heading, namely that of perfume — a heading not out of keeping with the life of a man always trim and pumiced.
11.24. It was resolved, on Cornutus's motion, that he be dealt with at the next session of the Senate; for then, whether by chance or by guilt, he had been absent.
11.25. You have the affairs of the city; in turn write me those of the country. How fare your little trees, your vines, your crops, your most delicate sheep? In short, unless you send back an equally long letter, you have no reason to expect henceforth anything but the very shortest. Farewell.
12.1. That little business, which I lately wrote remained over from the case of Marius Priscus, has been, I know not whether sufficiently, yet pared down and shaved away.
12.2. Firminus, brought into the Senate, answered to a known charge. There followed divergent opinions from the consuls-elect. Cornutus Tertullus moved that he be expelled from the order; Acutius Nerva, that in the allotment of a province his name be left out of account. This latter opinion, as the milder, prevailed, though it is in fact harsher and more grievous.
12.3. For what is more wretched than to be cut off and removed from senatorial honours, yet not from their toil and trouble? What is heavier than, branded with such great ignominy, not to lie hidden in solitude, but to be set on this loftiest watchtower to be looked at and pointed out?
12.4. Besides, what is publicly less either fitting or seemly? to sit, censured by the Senate, in the Senate, and to be made equal to those very men by whom one has been censured; to have been removed from a proconsulship because he had behaved disgracefully on a legateship, and yet to judge concerning proconsuls; and, condemned of corruption, either to condemn or to acquit others!
12.5. But this seemed best to the majority. For opinions are counted, not weighed; nor can anything else be done in a public council, in which nothing is so unequal as equality itself. For though wisdom is unequal, the right of all is equal.

title: Letters
text:
12.6. I have fulfilled my promise and discharged the pledge of my earlier letter, which from the lapse of time I conclude you have by now received; for I gave it to a hasty and careful courier, unless he met with some hindrance on the road.
12.7. It is now your part to requite, first that letter, then this one, with letters as rich as can come back from where you are. Farewell.
13.1. Both you most eagerly embrace occasions of obliging me, and I owe a debt to no one more gladly.
13.2. For two reasons, therefore, I have resolved to ask of you in particular what I most desire to obtain. You command a very large army: hence you have abundant material for benefits, and besides a long time in which you have been able to grace your friends. Turn now to ours — and these not many.
13.3. You indeed would prefer many; but my modesty is content with one or two, and rather with one.
13.4. He will be Voconius Romanus. His father was famous in the equestrian rank, more famous his stepfather — or rather his other father, for to this name too he succeeded by his devotion — his mother of the first families. He himself was lately the priest of Nearer Spain — you know what the judgment of that province is, how great its gravity.
13.5. Him I loved closely and intimately when we studied together; he was my companion in the city, my companion in retreat; with him I mingled serious matters, with him jests.
13.6. For what is more faithful than such a friend, more pleasant than such a comrade? There is a wonderful sweetness in his speech, wonderful too in his very face and look.
13.7. To this is added a lofty, subtle, sweet, ready, and learned talent in pleading causes; his letters, indeed, he writes so that you would believe the Muses themselves were speaking Latin. He is loved by me exceedingly, and yet is not outdone in love.
13.8. Indeed, when we were young, I conferred upon him, young as he was, as eagerly as my age allowed, whatever I could; and lately I obtained for him from the best of princes the privilege of one who has three children — which, although he grants it sparingly and with discrimination, he yet bestowed on me as though he were making the choice himself.
13.9. These benefits of mine I can in no way better protect than by increasing them, especially since he himself interprets them so gratefully that, while receiving the former, he earns the latter.
13.10. You have what manner of man, how approved and dear to me, is he whom I ask you to grace according to your character and your fortune. Above all, love the man; for though you bestow on him the most that you can, you can yet bestow nothing greater than your friendship; that he is capable of this even to the most intimate familiarity — that you might know it the better — I have briefly set out for you his pursuits, his character, in short his whole life.
13.11. I would prolong my entreaties, but that you do not wish to be asked at length, and that I have done this through the whole letter; for he asks, and most effectively, who gives the reasons for asking. Farewell.
14.1. You opine truly: I am distracted by cases in the Court of the Hundred, which exercise me more than they delight me. For most of them are small and trifling; rarely does one occur distinguished either by the eminence of the persons or the magnitude of the matter.
14.2. To this is added that there are few with whom it is a pleasure to speak; the rest are bold and, for the most part, obscure youths who have come over here to declaim, so irreverently and rashly that our friend Atilius seems to me to have put it pointedly when he said that boys begin in the Forum with cases in the Court of the Hundred as they begin with Homer in the schools. For here too, as there, what is greatest is the first thing they take up.

title: Letters
text:
14.3. But, by Hercules, before my time — so their elders are wont to say — not even the noblest youths had a place there unless brought forward by some consular: with such great reverence was that fairest of pursuits cultivated.
14.4. Now, the barriers of modesty and reverence broken down, all things lie open to all, and men are not led in but burst in. There follow hearers like the speakers, hired and bought. The dealer is approached; in the middle of the basilica the doles are given as openly as in a dining room; from court to court men pass at the same wage.
14.5. Hence they are now called, not without wit, "Sophocleses," from "wise" and "being called"; and on these same men a Latin name has been imposed, "Laudiceni" — the diners-out for applause;
14.6. and yet day by day the foulness grows, branded in both tongues. Yesterday two of my nomenclators — they are of the age of those who have lately assumed the toga — were being drawn off to applaud at three denarii apiece. So much it costs to be reckoned most eloquent. At this price the benches, however numerous, are filled; at this a huge ring of listeners is gathered; at this endless shouts are raised, when the leader of the chorus has given the signal.
14.7. For a signal is needed among men who do not understand, who do not even listen;
14.8. for most do not listen, and none applaud more. If ever you pass through the basilica and wish to know how each man speaks, there is no reason for you to mount the tribunal, none to lend your ear; the divination is easy: know that he speaks worst who is most applauded.
14.9. Larcius Licinus first introduced this fashion of listening, but only so far as to invite hearers. So at least I remember to have heard from Quintilian, my teacher.
14.10. He used to tell this story: "I attended Domitius Afer. When he was speaking before the Court of the Hundred, gravely and slowly — for that was his manner of pleading — he hears from nearby an immoderate and unusual shout. Astonished, he fell silent; when silence was made, he resumed what he had broken off.
14.11. Again the shout, again he was silent, and after the silence began again. The same a third time. At last he asked who was speaking. The answer was: 'Licinus.' Then, breaking off his case, 'Gentlemen of the Hundred,' he said, 'this art is dead.'"
14.12. Which was even then beginning to die when it seemed to Afer to have died, but now is well-nigh utterly extinguished and overthrown. I am ashamed to report with what broken delivery things are spoken, and with what soft shouts they are received.
14.13. Only the clapping is lacking — or rather only the cymbals and drums are lacking to those chantings; for howls — for by no other word can a praise unseemly even for the theatres be expressed — there are abundantly to spare.
14.14. Yet so far both the interest of my friends and the consideration of my age delays and detains me; for I am afraid that I may seem not to have left these indignities behind, but to have fled from labour. Still, I am rarer there than usual, which is the beginning of a gradual leaving off. Farewell.
15.1. How do your old Marsian estates treat you? how the new purchase? Do the lands please now that they have become yours? That is rare indeed; for nothing is so welcome to us when we have gained it as when we were coveting it.
15.2. My mother's estates treat me too little kindly, yet they delight me as my mother's, and besides I have grown callous with long endurance. Constant complaints have this end, that one is ashamed to complain. Farewell.

title: Letters
text:
16.1. You indeed, with your usual diligence, advise me that the codicils of Acilianus, who made me heir to part of his estate, should be held as unwritten, because they are not confirmed by the will;
16.2. which point of law is not unknown even to me, since it is known even to those who know nothing else. But I have laid down a certain law of my own, to maintain the wishes of the dead, even if they fail in point of law, as though they were perfected. Now it is established that these codicils were written in Acilianus's own hand.
16.3. Therefore, although they are not confirmed by the will, by me they shall be observed as if confirmed, especially since there is no room for an informer.
16.4. For if it were to be feared that what I gave the State might snatch away, I ought perhaps to be more hesitant and cautious; but since an heir is permitted to give away what has come to him by inheritance, there is nothing to stand in the way of that law of mine, with which the public laws do not conflict. Farewell.
17.1. You wonder why my Laurentine villa — or, if you prefer, my Laurens — delights me so much; you will cease to wonder when you learn the charm of the villa, the convenience of the place, the extent of the shore.
17.2. It is seventeen miles distant from the city, so that, when the business that had to be done is finished, you can stay there with the day still safe and ordered. It is reached by more than one road; for both the Laurentine and the Ostian lead to the same place, but the Laurentine must be left at the fourteenth milestone, the Ostian at the eleventh. From both directions a road partly sandy receives you, somewhat heavier and longer for carriages, but short and soft for a horse.
17.3. The scene is varied on this side and that; for now the road is narrowed by woods that meet it, now it spreads out and opens across very wide meadows; there are many flocks of sheep, many herds of horses and cattle, which, driven down from the mountains in winter, grow sleek in the grass and the warmth of spring. The villa is roomy for its uses, yet not costly to keep up.
17.4. In its front part is a frugal but not mean atrium; then a colonnade curved into the likeness of the letter D, by which a small but cheerful court is enclosed. This is an excellent refuge against storms; for it is protected by glazed windows and, still more, by the overhanging eaves.
17.5. Opposite its middle is a cheerful inner hall, then a fairly handsome dining room, which runs out toward the shore and, when the sea is driven by the southwest wind, is lightly washed by the now broken and last of the waves. On every side it has folding doors or windows no smaller than the doors, and so from the sides and the front it looks out, as it were, on three seas; at the back it looks back upon the inner hall, the colonnade, the court, the colonnade again, then the atrium, the woods, and the distant mountains.
17.6. To the left of this, set a little back, is a large bedroom, then another smaller one which admits the rising sun by one window and keeps the setting sun by another; by this latter it also looks down upon the sea below, more distant indeed but safer.
17.7. By the projection of this bedroom and that dining room a corner is enclosed which holds and kindles the purest sunshine. This is the winter retreat, this also the exercise ground of my household; here all the winds are silent, except those which bring clouds, and take away the clear weather before they take away the use of the place.

title: Letters
text:
17.8. To this corner is joined a bedroom curved into an apse, which by all its windows follows the course of the sun. Into its wall is set a cabinet, in the likeness of a library, which holds books not to be read once but read again and again.
17.9. Adjoining is a sleeping chamber, with a passage between, which, raised on a floor with hot-air pipes, distributes and dispenses the gathered heat hither and thither at a healthful temperature. The remaining part of this wing is given over to the use of slaves and freedmen, most of it so neat that it could receive guests.
17.10. On the other side is a most elegant bedroom; then either a large bedroom or a moderate dining hall, which shines with abundant sun and abundant sea; after this a bedroom with an antechamber, by its height summery, by its defences wintry; for it is sheltered from all the winds. To this bedroom another, with an antechamber, is joined by a common wall.
17.11. Next is the cold room of the bath, spacious and ample, in whose opposite walls two basins curve out, as it were, projecting — abundantly capacious if you consider that the sea is close by. Adjoining is the anointing room, the furnace room, adjoining the bath's stoke-hole, then two chambers more elegant than costly; close to these is joined a marvellous hot pool, from which the swimmers look upon the sea,
17.12. and not far off a ball court which catches the hottest sun when the day is now declining. Here a tower rises, beneath which are two suites of rooms, as many in the tower itself, and besides a dining room which commands the widest sea, the longest shore, and the most charming villas.
17.13. There is another tower too; in this is a bedroom in which the sun rises and sets; behind it a broad storeroom and granary, beneath this a dining room, which feels nothing of a troubled sea but its crash and sound, and that now languid and dying away; it looks upon the garden and the riding ground by which the garden is enclosed.
17.14. The riding ground is bordered with box, or with rosemary where the box fails; for the box, in the part where it is sheltered by buildings, is abundantly green, but under the open sky and the open wind, and though the sea's spray reach it only from afar, it withers.
17.15. Adjoining the riding ground, on its inner circuit, is a vine, tender and shady, soft and yielding even to bare feet. The garden the mulberry and the fig, which are frequent there, clothe; of these trees that soil is most fruitful, though more grudging to the rest. With this view, no worse than the sea's, the dining room remote from the sea enjoys itself; it is girdled at the back by two suites, from whose windows lie below the vestibule of the villa and another garden, rich and rustic.
17.16. From here a covered colonnade, almost of public dimensions, stretches out. On either side are windows, more toward the sea, single ones toward the garden, but on alternate sides fewer. These, when the day is clear and still, all lie open; when it is troubled by winds on this side or that, they lie open without harm on the side where the winds are quiet.
17.17. Before the covered colonnade is a terrace fragrant with violets. The warmth of the sun poured upon it the colonnade increases by reflection; and as it holds the sun, so it checks and keeps off the north wind, and there is as much cold behind as warmth in front; in like manner it stays the southwest wind, and so breaks and ends the most opposite winds, the one on this side, the other on that. This is its pleasantness in winter, greater in summer.

title: Letters
text:
17.18. For before noon it tempers with its shade the terrace, after noon the nearest part of the riding ground and garden; which shade, as the day grows or wanes, falls now shorter, now longer, on this side or that.
17.19. The covered colonnade itself is most free from sun just when it stands hottest upon its roof. Besides, with its windows open it receives and lets through the west winds, and is never oppressive with a sluggish and stagnant air.
17.20. At the head of the terrace, then of the covered colonnade and the garden, is a suite, my darling — truly my darling: I built it myself. In it is a sun parlour, which faces by one side the terrace, by another the sea, by both the sun; while the bedroom looks by its folding doors upon the colonnade, by its window upon the sea.
17.21. Opposite the middle wall a most elegant alcove recedes, which, by drawing forward or back its glazed panels and curtains, is now added to the bedroom, now taken away. It holds a couch and two chairs; at the feet is the sea, at the back the villas, at the head the woods: so many views of places it both distinguishes and mingles by as many windows.
17.22. Joined to this is a bedroom for night and sleep. Neither the voices of the young slaves, nor the murmur of the sea, nor the motions of storms, nor the flash of lightnings, nor even the day does it feel, unless the windows are open. The reason for this deep and hidden seclusion is that an intervening corridor separates the wall of the bedroom from the garden, and so consumes all sound in the empty space between.
17.23. Attached to the bedroom is a very small heated room, which by a narrow window either pours out or holds in the heat beneath it, as reason requires. From here an antechamber and bedroom stretch out toward the sun, which, caught at its rising, it keeps even past noon, slanting indeed, but still.
17.24. When I have withdrawn into this suite, I seem to be away even from my own villa, and I take great pleasure in it, especially at the Saturnalia, when the rest of the house rings with the license of the days and the festive shouts; for neither do I disturb my household's games, nor they my studies.
17.25. This usefulness, this charm, lacks only running water; but it has wells, or rather springs; for they are right at the surface. And altogether the nature of that shore is wonderful: in whatever spot you dig the ground, water meets you, ready and waiting, and that pure and not in the least spoiled, despite so great a nearness of the sea.
17.26. The neighbouring woods supply wood in abundance; the rest of the supplies the colony of Ostia provides. For a frugal man, indeed, even the village suffices, which a single villa separates from us. In it are three hired baths, a great convenience, if by chance a sudden arrival or too short a stay makes it inadvisable to heat the bath at home.
17.27. The shore is adorned, with a most pleasing variety, now by continuous, now by scattered roofs of villas, which present the appearance of many cities, whether you use the sea or the very shore; the shore which sometimes a long calm softens, more often the frequent and contrary surge hardens.
17.28. The sea does not, indeed, abound in costly fish, yet it casts up excellent soles and prawns. Our villa, moreover, provides even inland supplies, milk above all; for thither the herds gather from the pastures, whenever they seek water or shade.
17.29. Do I not seem to you, with just cause, now to dwell, to inhabit, to love this retreat? You are too much a townsman if you do not covet it. And would that you might covet it! so that to the many and great endowments of our little villa the greatest recommendation might be added from your company. Farewell.

title: Letters
text:
18.1. What more pleasant charge could you have laid upon me than to seek out a teacher for your brother's children? For by your kindness I go back to school, and, as it were, take up again that sweetest age: I sit among the young as I used to, and I even find how much authority I have with them from my studies.
18.2. For lately, in a crowded lecture room, they were joking aloud among themselves before many of our order; I came in, they fell silent; which I should not mention, except that it pertains more to their praise than to mine, and unless I wished you to hope that your brother's sons can learn well.
18.3. For the rest, when I have heard all who teach, I will write what I think of each, and will bring it about, so far as a letter can accomplish it, that you may seem yourself to have heard them all.
18.4. For I owe you, I owe to the memory of your brother, this fidelity, this zeal, especially in so great a matter. For what is of more concern to you than that the children — I would say yours, did you not now love them the more — should be found worthy of that father, and of you their uncle? a care which, even had you not enjoined it, I should have claimed for myself.
18.5. Nor am I unaware that offences must be incurred in choosing a teacher; but it behoves me to undergo not only offences but even enmities, on behalf of your brother's sons, with as even a mind as parents do on behalf of their own. Farewell.
19.1. You urge me to recite a speech to a larger circle of friends. I will do it because you urge it, although I have grave doubts.
19.2. For it does not escape me that speeches which are recited lose all their force and heat, and almost their very name, since they are wont to be commended and at the same time kindled by the gathering of the jurors, the throng of advocates, the expectation of the outcome, the reputation of more than one speaker, and the divided zeal of the hearers; and to this, the speaker's gesture, his pacing, even his moving about, and a vigour of body in keeping with all the motions of the mind.
19.3. Hence it happens that those who plead seated, although for the most part the same advantages remain to them as to those standing, are yet, by the mere fact that they sit, as it were weakened and depressed.
19.4. But for those who recite, the chief aids of delivery, the eyes and hands, are hindered. So it is the less to be wondered at if the attention of the hearers grows languid, captivated by no blandishments from without, nor roused by any goads.
19.5. To these is added that the speech of which I speak is combative and, as it were, contentious. Moreover, it is so ordained by nature that we think what we have written with labour is also heard with labour.
19.6. And indeed how few hearers are so upright that these sweet and sonorous things do not please them more than the austere and compressed? There is, to be sure, an altogether base discord here; yet it exists, because it commonly happens that the hearers demand one thing and the jurors another, although otherwise the hearer ought especially to be affected by those things by which, were he the juror, he would be most moved.
19.7. Yet it may happen that, despite these difficulties, novelty lends a charm to this book — novelty among our own people; for among the Greeks there is something which, though from the opposite side, is yet not altogether unlike.
19.8. For as it was their custom to refute the laws which they alleged to be contrary to earlier laws by comparison with others, so it was for us to gather, both from this very law and from others, that what we demanded was contained in the law of extortion; which, by no means pleasing to the ears of the ignorant, ought to find so much greater favour with the learned, as it finds less with the unlearned.

title: Letters
text:
19.9. But if we decide to recite, we shall call in all the most learned. Still, weigh with yourself whether it should be recited at all, set down all the considerations I have moved on both sides, and choose that in which reason prevails. For of you reason will be demanded; me my compliance will excuse. Farewell.
20.1. Get ready a penny and receive a golden tale — tales, rather; for the new one has reminded me of the old, and it does not matter with which I begin.
20.2. Verania, wife of Piso — I mean that Piso whom Galba adopted — was lying gravely ill. To her came Regulus. First, the impudence of the man, to come to a sick woman, to whose husband he had been a bitter enemy, and to herself most hateful!
20.3. Be it so, if he had only come; but he even sat down close by the couch, and asked on what day and at what hour she had been born. When he heard, he composes his face, fixes his eyes, moves his lips, works his fingers, reckons. Nothing. When he had long held the poor woman in suspense, "You have," he said, "a critical time, but you will come through it.
20.4. And that this may be clearer to you, I will consult a soothsayer, whom I have often tested."
20.5. No delay: he makes a sacrifice, affirms that the entrails agree with the indication of the stars. She, credulous as one in peril, asks for the codicils and writes a legacy to Regulus. Soon she grows worse, and dying cries out that the man is wicked, perfidious, and even worse than perjured, who had sworn falsely to her by the life of his son.
20.6. This Regulus does no less wickedly than frequently, that he calls down the wrath of the gods, whom he himself daily deceives, upon the head of his unhappy boy.
20.7. Velleius Blaesus, that rich man of consular rank, was struggling in his last illness: he wished to change his will. Regulus, who hoped for something from the new tablets, because he had lately begun to angle for him, kept exhorting and begging the physicians to prolong the man's breath by any means whatever.
20.8. After the will was sealed, he changes his part, turns his address, and to the same physicians: "How long will you torture the poor man? Why grudge a good death to one to whom you cannot give life?" Blaesus dies and, as though he had heard all, left Regulus not even the least thing.
20.9. Do two tales suffice, or, by the rule of the schools, do you demand a third? There is matter for it.
20.10. Aurelia, a woman of distinction, about to seal her will, had put on her most beautiful tunics. When Regulus had come to the sealing, "I beg you," he said, "leave these to me."
20.11. Aurelia thought the man was joking; he insisted in earnest. To be brief, he compelled the woman to open the tablets and bequeath to him the tunics she had on; he watched her writing, looked to see whether she had written it. And Aurelia, indeed, is alive; yet he forced that upon her as though she were about to die. And this man accepts inheritances, accepts legacies, as though he deserved them.
20.12. But why do I exert myself in a state in which for a long time now baseness and wickedness have won no smaller rewards — nay, greater — than modesty and virtue?
20.13. Look at Regulus, who from a poor and slender beginning has advanced, through crimes, to such great wealth that he himself told me, when he was consulting how soon he would complete sixty million sesterces, that he had found double entrails, by which it was portended that he would have a hundred and twenty million.
20.14. And he will have it, if only, as he has begun, he dictates other men's wills — which is the most wicked kind of forgery — to the very persons whose wills they are. Farewell.

title: Letters
text:
1.1. I do not know whether I have ever spent any time more agreeably than recently with Spurinna — so much so that there is no one I would more gladly imitate in old age, if indeed it be granted me to grow old; for nothing is more orderly than that manner of life.
1.2. To me, indeed, as the fixed course of the stars, so a well-arranged human life is a delight; and of old men especially. For while in the young a certain confusion and, as it were, disorder is not unbecoming, to old men all that is calm and ordered is fitting, in whom late activity and untimely ambition are unseemly.
1.3. This rule Spurinna keeps most steadfastly; indeed, even these small matters — small only if they are not done daily — he carries through in a certain order and as in a cycle.
1.4. In the morning he keeps to his couch; at the second hour he calls for his shoes, walks three miles, and exercises his mind no less than his body. If friends are present, the most honourable conversation is carried on; if not, a book is read, and sometimes too while friends are present, if only they do not find it tiresome.
1.5. Then he sits down, and again a book, or conversation better than a book; soon he mounts his carriage, taking with him his wife, a woman of singular excellence, or some one of his friends, as lately myself.
1.6. How fine, how sweet is that privacy! What antiquity is there! What deeds, what men you hear of! With what precepts you are imbued! — though he has imposed this temperate restraint on his own modesty, that he may not seem to lecture.
1.7. When seven miles have been completed, he walks again a mile, again sits down, or betakes himself to his bedchamber and his pen. For he writes, and in both tongues, lyric poems most learned; in them is a wonderful sweetness, wonderful charm, wonderful gaiety, whose grace is heightened by the purity of the writer.
1.8. When the hour of the bath is announced — it is in winter the ninth, in summer the eighth — he walks in the sun, if there is no wind, with nothing on. Then he plays ball vigorously and long; for by this kind of exercise too he fights against old age. When he has bathed, he lies down and puts off his meal a little while; meanwhile he listens to something read more lightly and sweetly. Through all this time it is free to his friends either to do the same or, if they prefer, something else.
1.9. A dinner is set on, no less elegant than frugal, on silver pure and antique; he has also Corinthian ware in use, in which he takes pleasure but is not enslaved to it. Frequently the dinner is varied by comedians, that even his pleasures may be seasoned with study. He takes something of the night, even in summer; to no one is this long, with such graciousness is the banquet prolonged.
1.10. Hence to him, after his seventy-seventh year, the vigour of ears and eyes is unimpaired; hence his body is agile and lively, and of old age he has only the wisdom.
1.11. This life I anticipate in wish and thought, ready to enter upon it most eagerly as soon as the consideration of my years shall permit me to sound the retreat. Meanwhile I am worn out by a thousand labours, of which this same Spurinna is to me both the solace and the example;
1.12. for he too, as long as it was honourable, discharged his duties, held magistracies, governed provinces, and by much labour earned this leisure. Therefore I set myself the same course, the same goal, and even now I subscribe it before you, so that, if you see me carried further, you may summon me to court by this very letter of mine, and bid me rest, when I shall have escaped the charge of sloth. Farewell.

title: Letters
text:
2.1. What I myself would have offered to your friends, had the same opportunity been mine, I now seem to have a right to ask of you for mine.
2.2. Arrianus Maturus is the foremost man of Altinum; when I say foremost, I do not speak of his means, which he has amply to spare, but of his purity, his justice, his gravity, his prudence.
2.3. His counsel I use in business, his judgment in my studies; for he excels above all in faithfulness, in truthfulness, in understanding.
2.4. He loves me — I can say nothing more ardent — as you do. He is without ambition; therefore he has kept himself in the equestrian rank, though he might easily rise to the highest. Yet by me he must be honoured and advanced.
2.5. And so I count it a great thing to add something to his standing, when he does not expect it, does not know of it — nay, perhaps even does not wish it; but to add something that is splendid and not troublesome.
2.6. Of which kind, the first opportunity that offers, I beg you to bestow upon him; you will have me, you will have himself, a most grateful debtor. For although he does not seek such things, yet he receives them as gratefully as if he coveted them. Farewell.
3.1. Since I doubt whether I looked up to your father, a most grave and holy man, more than I loved him, and since I love you uniquely, both in memory of him and for your own honour, I must needs desire, and even strive so far as in me lies, that your son should turn out like his grandfather — his maternal grandfather, I mean, although a paternal one too, famous and esteemed, fell to his lot, and his father and uncle also conspicuous in illustrious praise.
3.2. To all of whom he will grow up like only on this condition, that he be imbued with honourable arts; and it matters very much from whom above all he receives them.
3.3. Hitherto the reckoning of childhood has kept him within your household; he has had teachers at home, where there is little or even no material for error. Now his studies must be carried beyond the threshold, now a Latin rhetorician must be looked for, in whose school severity, modesty, and above all chastity are assured.
3.4. For there is present in our young man, with the other gifts of nature and fortune, an exceptional beauty of body, for which, in this slippery time of life, not only a teacher but a guardian and director too must be sought.
3.5. I think, then, that I can point out to you Iulius Genitor. He is loved by me; yet my affection for the man, which was born of judgment, does not stand in the way of my judgment. He is a man of correct and grave character, even a little rough and hard, as goes with this license of the times.
3.6. How much he is worth in eloquence you can take on the word of many, for the faculty of speaking, being open and exposed, is seen at once; but men's lives have deep recesses and great hiding places, for which, on behalf of Genitor, take me as surety. Nothing will your son hear from this man but what will profit him, nothing will he learn which it would have been better not to have known; and no less often than by you and me will he be reminded by him with what images he is laden, what names and how great he bears upon him.
3.7. So, with the gods favouring, hand him over to a teacher from whom he may learn first character, then eloquence, which is ill learned without character. Farewell.
4.1. Although both the friends I had present, and the talk of men, seem to have approved my deed, yet I count it a great thing to know what you think.

title: Letters
text:
4.2. For of one whose counsel I should have wished to seek out while the matter was untouched, I now wondrously long to know the judgment even when it is done. When I had hurried off into Tuscany, intending to begin a public work at my own expense, having obtained leave of absence as prefect of the treasury, the deputies of the province of Baetica, about to complain of the proconsulship of Caecilius Classicus, asked the Senate for me as their advocate.
4.3. My colleagues, men most excellent and most loving to me, having first spoken of the demands of our common duty, tried to excuse and exempt me. A decree of the Senate was passed, most honourable to me, that I should be given to the provincials as their patron if I obtained it from myself.
4.4. The deputies, brought in again, a second time demanded me, now present, as their advocate, imploring my good faith, of which they had had experience against Massa Baebius, and alleging the bond of patronage. There followed a most glorious assent of the Senate, such as is wont to forerun its decrees. Then I said: "I cease, conscript fathers, to think that I have brought forward just causes for excuse." Both the modesty of my speech and its reasoning were approved.
4.5. What drove me to this resolve was not only the consensus of the Senate, although this above all, but certain other and lesser considerations, yet still of some account. It came to mind that our forefathers had pursued, by voluntary accusations, even the wrongs done to single guest-friends; whence I thought it the more disgraceful to neglect the rights of a public guest-friendship.
4.6. Besides, when I recalled how many perils I had undergone, on a former advocacy, on behalf of these same people of Baetica, it seemed that the merit of an old service must be preserved by a new one. For it is so ordered that you overturn earlier benefits unless you heap them up with later ones. For however often men have been obliged, if you refuse one single thing, this alone they remember, that it was refused.
4.7. I was led also by the fact that Classicus had died, and that which in cases of this kind is wont to be most painful, the peril of a senator, was removed. I saw, then, that my advocacy had before it no less gratitude than if he were living, and no odium.
4.8. In short, I reckoned that if I discharged this office now for a third time, my excuse would be the easier, should someone come along whom I ought not to accuse. For since there is some limit to all duties, so indulgence is best prepared for one's freedom by past compliance.
4.9. You have heard the motions of my resolve: it remains for your judgment, on the one side or the other, in which the frankness of one who dissents will be as pleasant to me as the authority of one who approves. Farewell.
5.1. It is most gratifying to me that you read so diligently the books of my uncle, that you wish to have them all, and ask what they all are.
5.2. I will play the part of an index, and even make known to you in what order they were written; for this too is a knowledge not unpleasing to the studious.
5.3. "On Throwing the Javelin from Horseback, one book"; this he composed with equal talent and care while serving as prefect of a cavalry wing. "On the Life of Pomponius Secundus, two books"; by whom he was singularly loved, he discharged this gift, as it were a debt, to the memory of his friend.
5.4. "The Wars of Germany, twenty books"; in which he gathered together all the wars we waged with the Germans. He began it while serving in Germany, warned by a dream: the likeness of Drusus Nero stood by him as he slept — Drusus, who, after conquering the widest tracts of Germany, perished there — and commended his memory to him, begging that he might be rescued from the wrong of oblivion.

title: Letters
text:
5.5. "The Student, three books," divided, because of their length, into six volumes, in which he forms and perfects the orator from the cradle. "On Doubtful Diction, eight books": he wrote it under Nero in his last years, when servitude had made every kind of study, a little freer and bolder, dangerous.
5.6. "A Continuation of Aufidius Bassus, thirty-one books." "The Natural Histories, thirty-seven books," a diffuse and learned work, no less various than Nature herself.
5.7. You wonder that a busy man finished so many volumes, and many of them so minute in their detail? You will wonder the more if you learn that for some time he pleaded causes, that he died in his fifty-sixth year, and that the intervening time he passed taken up and hindered both by the greatest offices and by the friendship of princes.
5.8. But he had a keen mind, an incredible application, the utmost wakefulness. He used to begin to work by lamplight at the Vulcanalia, not for the sake of any omen but for study, straight from the dead of night; in winter from the seventh hour, or at latest the eighth, often the sixth. He was indeed of a most ready sleep, which sometimes even amid his very studies came upon him and then left him.
5.9. Before daylight he went to the emperor Vespasian — for he too made use of the nights — and thence to the duty assigned him. Returning home, he gave what time was left to his studies.
5.10. After his meal — which by day, in the manner of the ancients, he took light and easy — in summer, if there was any leisure, he would lie in the sun, a book would be read, he made notes and extracts. For he read nothing without making extracts; he used even to say that there was no book so bad that it was not useful in some part.
5.11. After the sun he generally bathed in cold water, then took a snack and slept a very little; soon, as though it were another day, he studied until dinnertime. Over this a book was read and noted, and indeed rapidly.
5.12. I remember that one of his friends, when the reader had pronounced certain words wrongly, called him back and made him repeat them; and my uncle said to him: "You understood, did you not?" When the man nodded, "Why then did you call him back? By this interruption of yours we have lost more than ten lines."
5.13. So great was his thrift of time. He rose in summer from dinner by daylight, in winter within the first hour of night, as though compelled by some law.
5.14. This in the midst of his labours and the din of the city. In his retreat only the time of the bath was taken from his studies — when I say the bath, I speak of the inner part; for while he was being scraped and dried, he would listen to something or dictate.
5.15. On a journey, as though freed from other cares, he had leisure for this one thing: at his side a shorthand writer with a book and tablets, whose hands in winter were protected with mittens, that not even the harshness of the weather should snatch any time from study; for which reason at Rome too he was carried in a chair.
5.16. I recall that I was reproved by him for walking: "You could," he said, "not have lost these hours"; for he thought all time lost that was not spent on study.
5.17. By this application he completed all those volumes, and left me a hundred and sixty notebooks of extracts, written on both sides and in the smallest hand; by which means the number is multiplied. He used to relate that, when he was procurator in Spain, he could have sold these notebooks to Larcius Licinus for four hundred thousand sesterces; and then they were somewhat fewer.

title: Letters
text:
5.18. Does it not seem to you, when you reflect how much he read, how much he wrote, that he was neither in any offices nor in the friendship of a prince? And again, when you hear how much labour he spent on study, that he neither wrote nor read enough? For what is there that either those occupations could not hinder, or this application not accomplish?
5.19. And so I am wont to laugh when certain men call me studious, who, compared with him, am the idlest of men. But I — whom partly public, partly my friends' affairs distract? Which of those who sit at their books all their life, set beside him, would not blush as one given over to sleep and inactivity?
5.20. I have prolonged this letter, though I had intended to write only what you asked, namely what books he had left behind; yet I am confident that these things too will be no less welcome to you than the books themselves, which may rouse you, by the goads of emulation, not only to read them but to work out something of the like. Farewell.
6.1. Out of an inheritance that came to me I lately bought a Corinthian statue, small indeed, but pleasing and lifelike, so far as I understand such things — I who in everything, perhaps, and in this certainly, understand very little: yet this statue even I can appreciate.
6.2. For it is naked, and neither hides any faults, if there are any, nor displays the merits too little. It represents an old man standing; the bones, muscles, sinews, veins, even the wrinkles appear as of a living man; the hair is thin and receding, the brow broad, the face shrunken, the neck lean; the arms hang, the breast is fallen, the belly drawn in;
6.3. from behind, too, the same age, as from behind. The bronze itself, so far as the true colour shows, is old and ancient; in short, everything is such as might hold the eyes of artists and delight the ignorant.
6.4. Which, novice though I am, prompted me to buy it. I bought it, however, not to keep at home — for I have as yet no Corinthian piece at home — but to set up in our native town, in a frequented place, and most of all in the temple of Jupiter;
6.5. for it seems a gift worthy of the temple, worthy of the god. Do you therefore, as you are wont to do with everything I lay upon you, take up this charge, and order even now a base to be made, of whatever marble you will, to receive my name and offices, if you shall think these too should be added.
6.6. The statue itself, as soon as I find someone who will not find it a burden, I will send you, or — which you prefer — bring myself along with me. For I intend, if only the reckoning of my duties permits, to make an excursion thither.
6.7. You rejoice that I promise to come, but you will knit your brow when I add "for a few days": for the same matters that do not yet let me come out do not let me be away longer. Farewell.
7.1. Just now it has been announced that Silius Italicus has ended his life by starvation in his Neapolitan villa.
7.2. The cause of his death was his health. There had grown upon him an incurable tumour, in weariness of which he ran down to death with irrevocable constancy, blessed and fortunate to his last day, except that he lost the younger of his two children, but left the elder and better one flourishing and even of consular rank.
7.3. He had harmed his reputation under Nero — he was believed to have brought accusations of his own accord — but in the friendship of Vitellius he had borne himself wisely and courteously, had won glory from his proconsulship of Asia, and had washed away the stain of his old activity by a praiseworthy leisure.

title: Letters
text:
7.4. He was among the leading men of the state without power, without odium: he was greeted and courted, and, lying much upon his couch, always in a bedchamber thronged not by his fortune's sake, he passed his days in most learned conversation, when he was at leisure from writing.
7.5. He wrote poems with more care than talent, and sometimes tested men's judgments by recitations.
7.6. Latest of all, his years so counselling, he withdrew from the city, kept himself in Campania, and was not stirred from there even by the arrival of a new prince:
7.7. great praise to the Caesar under whom this was free, great to the man who dared to use this freedom.
7.8. He was a lover of beauty, even to the reproach of overbuying. He owned several villas in the same places, and, falling in love with new ones, neglected the earlier. Everywhere were many books, many statues, many portraits, which he not only possessed but even venerated — of Virgil before all, whose birthday he celebrated more religiously than his own, especially at Naples, where he was wont to visit his monument as a temple.
7.9. In this tranquillity he passed his seventy-fifth year, with a body delicate rather than infirm; and as he was the last consul made by Nero, so he was the last to die of all whom Nero had made consuls.
7.10. This too is notable: he was the last of Nero's consulars to die, and it was in his consulship that Nero perished. Which, when I recall it, a pity for human frailty comes over me.
7.11. For what is so cut short, so brief, as the longest human life? Does not Nero seem to you to have been but yesterday? And yet, meanwhile, of those who held the consulship under him, no one now survives.
7.12. Yet why do I wonder at this? Lately Lucius Piso — the father of that Piso who was killed in Africa by Valerius Festus through the foulest of crimes — used to say that he saw no one in the Senate whom he himself, as consul, had asked his opinion.
7.13. Within such narrow bounds is the very long life of so great a multitude shut up, that those royal tears seem to me worthy not only of pardon but even of praise; for they say that Xerxes, when he had run his eyes over his immense army, wept, because so short a doom hung over so many thousands.
7.14. But all the more, this fleeting and perishable span, whatever it is, if it is not given to deeds — for the material of these lies in another's hand — at least let us prolong by our studies, and, since it is denied us to live long, let us leave behind something by which to bear witness that we have lived.
7.15. I know you have no need of spurs: yet my affection for you summons me to urge you on even while you run, as you are wont to do with me. "Strife is good" when friends, by mutual exhortations, sharpen one another to a love of immortality. Farewell.
8.1. You act in keeping with the rest of the regard you show me, in that you ask so anxiously that I transfer the tribunate, which I obtained for you from Neratius Marcellus, a most distinguished man, to your kinsman Caesennius Silvanus.
8.2. But to me, just as it was most pleasing to see you yourself a tribune, so it is no less welcome to see another through you. For I do not think it consistent that, of one whom you wish to advance with honours, you should grudge him the titles of family affection, which are fairer than all honours.
8.3. I see too that, since it is excellent both to earn benefits and to bestow them, you will gain both praises at once, if you bestow on another what you yourself have earned. Besides, I understand that it will be a glory to me also, if from this deed of yours it be not unknown that my friends can not only hold tribunates but even give them.

title: Letters
text:
8.4. Wherefore I indeed yield to your most honourable wish. For the name has not yet been entered on the rolls, and therefore it is free to us to substitute Silvanus in your place; to whom I hope your gift may be as welcome as mine is to you. Farewell.
9.1. I can now describe to you in full how much labour I expended in the public cause of the province of Baetica.
9.2. For it was manifold, and was pleaded several times with great variety. Whence the variety, whence the several pleadings? Caecilius Classicus — a foul man and openly bad — had conducted his proconsulship there no less violently than basely, in the same year in which Marius Priscus held his in Africa.
9.3. Now Priscus was from Baetica, Classicus from Africa. Hence a saying of the people of Baetica was going about, not without wit — for grief often makes men witty too — "I gave an evil and I got one."
9.4. But Marius one city publicly and many private persons brought to trial; upon Classicus the whole province bore down. He forestalled the accusation by a death whether accidental or voluntary. For his death was infamous, yet ambiguous: for as it seemed credible that he had wished to depart from life when he could not be defended, so it seemed strange that he had fled by death the shame of a condemnation which he had not been ashamed to deserve by his conduct.
9.6. Nonetheless Baetica persisted in the accusation even of the dead man. This is provided for by the laws, but had fallen into disuse, and after a long interval was then revived. The men of Baetica added that they accused at the same time the associates and ministers of Classicus, and demanded an inquiry into them by name.
9.7. I was acting for the Baetici, and with me Lucceius Albinus, a man fluent and ornate in speaking; whom, though I had long loved with a mutual affection, from this partnership of duty I began to love more ardently.
9.8. Glory, indeed, especially in studies, has a certain quality that brooks no partner; yet between us there was no rivalry, no contention, since each strove under an equal yoke not for himself but for the cause, whose greatness and usefulness seemed to demand that we should not take upon ourselves so great a burden in single pleadings.
9.9. We feared that the day, the voice, the lungs might fail us, if we embraced so many charges and so many defendants in one bundle, as it were; then, that the attention of the judges, with so many names and so many cases, would not only be wearied but even confounded; next, that the influence of individuals, collected and combined, might gain for each one the strength of all; and finally, that the most powerful might, by the surrender of some most worthless man as a scapegoat, slip away through the punishment of others.
9.10. For it is then most of all that favour and intrigue prevail, when they can lurk under some appearance of severity.
9.11. We had before us in council that example of Sertorius, who ordered the strongest and the weakest soldier to pluck out a horse's tail — the rest you know. For we too saw that so numerous a column of defendants could be overcome only if it were torn apart man by man.
9.12. It was resolved first of all to show Classicus himself guilty: this was the most fitting transition to his associates and ministers, since the associates and ministers could not be proved guilty unless he were guilty. Of these we at once joined two to Classicus, Baebius Probus and Fabius Hispanus, both strong in influence, Hispanus also in eloquence. And concerning Classicus the labour was short and easy.

title: Letters
text:
9.13. He had left written in his own hand what he had received from each transaction, from each case; he had even sent letters to Rome, to a certain mistress, boastful and vainglorious, in these very words: "Hurrah, hurrah, I come to you free; I have already realized four million sesterces by selling part of the Baetici."
9.14. About Hispanus and Probus there was much sweat. Before I entered upon their charges, I thought it necessary to labour to establish that the ministering itself was a crime: for unless I had done this, I should have proved them ministers in vain.
9.15. For they were not so defended as to deny it, but to pray pardon for their necessity; for they were provincials, and were driven by fear to every command of the proconsuls.
9.16. Claudius Restitutus, who replied to me — a man practised and vigilant and ready for whatever might suddenly arise — is wont to say that never was so much darkness, so much confusion poured upon him as when he saw snatched and wrested away from his defence those very things in which he had placed all his confidence.
9.17. The outcome of our counsel was this: the goods of Classicus, which he had had before his province, it pleased the Senate to separate from the rest, and to leave the former to his daughter, the latter to those he had despoiled. It was added that the moneys which he had paid to creditors should be recalled. Hispanus and Probus were banished for five years; so grave did that seem which at first was doubted to be a crime at all.
9.18. A few days later we accused Claudius Fuscus, the son-in-law of Classicus, and Stilonius Priscus, who had been tribune of a cohort under Classicus, with unequal outcome: Priscus was interdicted from Italy for two years; Fuscus was acquitted.
9.19. In the third pleading we thought it most convenient to gather several together, lest, if the inquiry were drawn out too long, by a kind of satiety and weariness the justice and severity of the judges should grow languid; and besides, there remained the lesser defendants, deliberately reserved for this place, with the exception, however, of the wife of Classicus, who, though entangled in suspicions, seemed not sufficiently convicted by proofs;
9.20. for the daughter of Classicus, who was herself among the defendants, was not held fast even by suspicions. And so, when I had come to her name in the last pleading — for there was no need to fear, as at the beginning, so also at the end, that by this the authority of the whole accusation might be diminished — I thought it most honourable not to press the undeserving, and I said this very thing, both freely and in various ways.
9.21. For now I asked the deputies whether they had taught me anything which they were confident could be proved by fact; now I sought counsel of the Senate whether it thought I ought, if I had any faculty in speaking, to aim it like some weapon at the throat of an innocent woman; finally I closed the whole passage with this conclusion: "Someone will say: Do you then pass judgment? I indeed do not judge; yet I remember that I was given as an advocate from among the judges."
9.22. This was the end of a most crowded case, some being acquitted, more condemned and even banished, some for a time, others for life.
9.23. By the same decree of the Senate our industry, fidelity, and constancy were attested in the fullest testimony — the only fit and equal reward for so great a labour.
9.24. You can conceive in your mind how wearied we were, who had so often to plead, so often to dispute, so many witnesses to question, to support, to refute.

title: Letters
text:
9.25. And how arduous, how troublesome it was, to refuse the friends of so many defendants who asked in secret, to withstand openly those who opposed us! I will report one thing among those I said. When certain of the very judges cried out against me on behalf of a most favoured defendant, "He will be," I said, "no less innocent, if I shall have said all."
9.26. From this you will guess what contentions, even what offences, we underwent, but only for a short time; for good faith, for the present, offends those whom it resists, but afterwards is admired and praised by those very men. I could not bring you more fully into the matter as it was.
9.27. You will say: "It was not worth so much; for what have I to do with so long a letter?" Then do not keep asking what is being done at Rome. And yet remember that it is not a long letter which has embraced so many days, so many inquiries, in short so many defendants and cases.
9.28. All which I seem to myself to have pursued no less briefly than diligently. I said "diligently" rashly: there comes to mind what I had passed over, and indeed late, but, though out of order, it shall be rendered. Homer does this, and many on his example; it is, moreover, very becoming, yet not on that account will it be done by me.
9.29. One of the witnesses, whether angry that he had been summoned against his will, or suborned by one of the defendants to disarm the accusation, charged Norbanus Licinianus, a deputy and investigator, as a defendant, on the ground that in the case of Casta — this is the wife of Classicus — he was acting in collusion.
9.30. It is provided by law that the defendant be tried first, and then inquiry be made about the collusive prosecutor — clearly because the good faith of an accuser is best estimated from the accusation itself.
9.31. Yet to Norbanus neither the order of the law, nor the name of deputy, nor the office of investigator was a protection; so great was the odium with which he blazed, a man otherwise disgraceful, and one who had made use of Domitian's times as many had, and who had been chosen then by the province to investigate not as a good and faithful man, but as an enemy of Classicus — for he had been banished by him.
9.32. He demanded that a day be granted him, that the charges be set out; he obtained neither, and was compelled to reply at once. He replied — the man's evil and crooked nature makes me doubt whether confidently or constantly, but certainly most readily.
9.33. Many things were thrown against him, which harmed him more than the collusion; indeed two consulars, Pomponius Rufus and Libo Frugi, wounded him by their testimony, that he had appeared, before a judge under Domitian, on the side of the accusers of Salvius Liberalis.
9.34. He was condemned and banished to an island. And so, when I accused Casta, I pressed nothing more than that her accuser had fallen under the charge of collusion; yet I pressed it in vain, for a thing contrary and new came to pass, that, the accuser of collusion being condemned, the defendant was acquitted.
9.35. You ask, what were we doing while these things went on? We informed the Senate that we had learned the public cause from Norbanus, and that we must learn it anew from the beginning if he were proved a collusive prosecutor; and so, while he was being tried as a defendant, we sat by. Afterwards Norbanus was present on all the days of the inquiry, and bore the same — whether constancy or audacity — to the very end.
9.36. I ask myself whether I have again omitted anything, and again I had almost omitted something. On the last day Salvius Liberalis gravely rebuked the remaining deputies, on the ground that they had not brought to trial all whom the province had charged them with; and, being vehement and eloquent, he brought them into peril. I protected men most excellent and most grateful: to me at least they declare that they owe it that they escaped that whirlwind.

title: Letters
text:
9.37. Here will be the end of the letter — really the end; I will not add a letter, even if I shall perceive that I have still passed something over. Farewell.
10.1. That I had composed something about your son I did not tell you, when I was lately with you, first because I had not written it in order to tell you, but to satisfy my own love, my own grief; then because I believed that you, Spurinna, having heard that I had recited, as you yourself told me, had heard at the same time what I had recited.
10.2. Besides, I was afraid of confounding you on your festal days, if I should bring back the memory of so grievous a sorrow. Now too I hesitated a little, whether to send only what I recited, as you require, or to add what I think of reserving for another volume.
10.3. For it is not enough for my affection to honour with one little book a memory most dear and most holy to me, whose fame will be more widely served if it be apportioned and arranged.
10.4. But as I hesitated whether to show you all that I have already composed, or still to put off some part, it seemed simpler and more friendly to show all, especially since you assure me that it will remain among yourselves until I am pleased to publish it.
10.5. For the rest, I ask that with equal frankness you point out to me whatever you shall think should be added, changed, or omitted.
10.6. It is difficult to bend the mind thus far amid grief; difficult, but yet, as you would admonish a sculptor or a painter who was making your son's likeness what he ought to express, what to correct, so do you too form and direct me, who am trying to make not a fragile and perishable, but, as you think, an immortal image: which will be the more lasting, the truer, the better, the more perfect it shall be. Farewell.
11.1. The nature of our friend Artemidorus is altogether so kindly that he exalts the services of friends beyond their worth. Hence even my merit, true though it is, he carries about with a praise beyond its merit.
11.2. Indeed, when the philosophers had been banished from the city, I was with him in his suburban villa, and — what made it the more notable, that is, the more dangerous — I was with him as praetor. Money too, of which he then had need in a larger amount, to pay off a debt contracted from the most honourable causes, while certain great and wealthy friends muttered, I myself borrowed and gave him free of interest.
11.3. And these things I did when seven of my friends had been either killed or banished — killed, Senecio, Rusticus, Helvidius; banished, Mauricus, Gratilla, Arria, Fannia — so many thunderbolts hurled around me that, as though scorched, I augured from certain sure signs that the same ruin hung over me too.
11.4. Yet I do not on that account believe that I deserved the exceptional glory which he proclaims, but only that I escaped disgrace.
11.5. For I both loved with admiration Gaius Musonius, his father-in-law, as far as my age allowed, and embraced Artemidorus himself, even then, when I was serving as military tribune in Syria, in close familiarity; and this I gave as the first token of no slight disposition, that I seemed to discern a man either wise or nearest and most like to wise.
11.6. For of all who now call themselves philosophers, you will scarcely find one or two of such sincerity, such truthfulness. I pass over with what patience of body he endures winters and summers alike, how he yields to no labours, how he allows nothing to pleasures in food or drink, how he keeps his eyes and his mind under control.

title: Letters
text:
11.7. These are great things, but in another; in him indeed the least, if they be compared with his other virtues, by which he deserved to be taken as son-in-law by Gaius Musonius out of all the followers of all ranks.
11.8. Which things, when I recall them, it is indeed pleasant that he heaps me with such great praises both before others and before you; yet I am afraid he may exceed the measure, which his kindness — for I return to where I began — is wont not to keep.
11.9. For in this one thing a man otherwise most prudent sometimes errs, by an honourable error indeed, in that he thinks his friends better than they are. Farewell.
12.1. I will come to dinner, but I bargain now, let it be light, let it be frugal, let it abound only in Socratic conversation, and in this too keep a measure.
12.2. There will be morning duties before daybreak, which not even Cato could fall in with unscathed — Cato, whom yet Gaius Caesar so blames as to praise.
12.3. For he describes those whom Cato met, when they had uncovered the head of the drunken man, as having blushed; then he adds: "You would think that not they had been caught by Cato, but Cato by them." Could more authority be given to Cato than that he was so venerable even when drunk?
12.4. Yet let our dinner keep a measure, of time as well as of preparation and expense. For we are not such men as even our enemies could blame, except so as at the same time to praise. Farewell.
13.1. The book in which I lately, as consul, gave thanks to the best of princes, I have sent at your demand, and would have sent even had you not demanded it.
13.2. In it I should like you to consider, as the beauty of the subject, so its difficulty. For in other works novelty itself holds the reader intent; in this all things are known, common, already said; whence it comes that the reader, as it were at leisure and free of care, has time only for the diction, in which it is harder to satisfy when it is estimated alone.
13.3. And would that at least the order and the transitions and the figures were considered along with it! For to invent splendidly, to express magnificently, even barbarians sometimes do; but to arrange aptly, to figure variously, is denied to all but the learned.
13.4. Nor indeed should lofty and elevated things always be affected. For as in a painting nothing commends the light more than shadow, so it becomes a speech to lower itself as well as to raise itself.
13.5. But why do I say these things to a most learned man? Rather this: note what you shall think should be corrected. For so I shall the more believe that the rest pleases you, if I learn that some things have displeased you. Farewell.
14.1. An atrocious thing, and worthy of more than a letter, Larcius Macedo, a man of praetorian rank, has suffered at the hands of his slaves — a proud master, moreover, and cruel, and one who remembered too little — nay, too much — that his own father had been a slave.
14.2. He was bathing in his villa at Formiae. Suddenly his slaves surround him. One seizes his throat, another strikes his face, another his chest and belly, and even — foul to tell — his private parts; and when they thought him lifeless, they fling him onto the burning pavement, to test whether he was alive. He, whether because he did not feel it, or because he feigned not to feel it, motionless and outstretched, made good the belief that death had been accomplished.
14.3. Then at last, as though overcome by the heat, he is carried out; the more faithful slaves take him up, his concubines run together with howling and outcry. So, both roused by their voices and revived by the coolness of the place, he raised his eyes and moved his body, and confessed — for now it was safe — that he was alive.

title: Letters
text:
14.4. The slaves scatter; a great part of them have been seized, the rest are being sought. He himself, with difficulty kept alive for a few days, died not without the consolation of vengeance, avenged while living as men commonly are when slain.
14.5. You see to how many perils, to how many affronts, to how many mockeries we are exposed; nor has anyone reason to feel safe because he is easygoing and mild; for it is not by the judgment of masters but by crime that they are destroyed.
14.6. But enough of this. What else is new? What? Nothing — otherwise I would add it; for both paper still remains, and the holiday allows more to be woven in. I will add what fittingly comes to mind about this same Macedo. When he was bathing in a public bath at Rome, a notable thing happened, and even, as the outcome showed, an ominous one.
14.7. A Roman knight, lightly admonished by his hand by one of Macedo's slaves to give passage, turned round and struck, not the slave by whom he had been touched, but Macedo himself, so heavily with his palm that he almost fell.
14.8. So the bath, by certain steps as it were, was to him first a place of affront, then of destruction. Farewell.
15.1. You ask that in my retreat I read and examine your little books, whether they are worthy of publication; you add entreaties, you allege a precedent: for you ask that I steal some spare time from my own studies and bestow it on yours, adding that Marcus Tullius fostered the talents of poets with wonderful kindness.
15.2. But I am neither to be asked nor exhorted; for I both venerate poetry itself most religiously and love you most exceedingly. I will do, then, what you desire, as diligently as gladly.
15.3. Yet I think I can write back even now that it is a fine work and not to be suppressed, so far as I could estimate from what you recited in my presence — if only your recitation did not impose upon me; for you read most sweetly and most skilfully.
15.4. Still, I am confident that I am not so led by the ears that all the stings of my judgment are broken by those charms: they are perhaps blunted and a little dulled, but they cannot be torn out and wrested away.
15.5. Therefore I do not rashly pronounce even now upon the whole; of the parts I will make trial by reading. Farewell.
16.1. I seem to have observed that some deeds and sayings of men and women are more famous, others greater. My opinion was confirmed by yesterday's conversation with Fannia. She is the granddaughter of that Arria who was to her husband both a solace in death and an example. She used to relate many things of her grandmother, no less great than this one but more obscure; which I think will be as wonderful to you in the reading as they were to me in the hearing.
16.3. Her husband Caecina Paetus was ill, ill too was her son, both mortally, as it seemed. The son died, of exceptional beauty and equal modesty, dear to his parents no less for other reasons than because he was their son. For him she so prepared the funeral, so conducted the obsequies, that her husband knew nothing of it; nay more, whenever she entered his chamber, she pretended that the son lived and was even better, and very often, when he asked how the boy did, she answered: "He has rested well, he has taken his food gladly." Then, when the tears she had long held back overcame her and burst forth, she went out; then she gave herself to grief; satisfied, with dry eyes and composed face she returned, as though she had left her bereavement outside. That deed of hers is famous indeed — to draw the sword, pierce her breast, draw out the dagger, hold it out to her husband, and add the immortal and almost divine words: "Paetus, it does not hurt." But yet, as she did this, as she said this, glory and eternity were before her eyes; how much greater it is, without the reward of eternity, without the reward of glory, to hide her tears, to cover her grief, and, with her son lost, still to play the mother.

title: Letters
text:
16.7. Scribonianus had taken up arms in Illyricum against Claudius; Paetus had been on his side, and, Scribonianus being killed, was being dragged to Rome. He was about to go aboard ship; Arria begged the soldiers that she might be put aboard with him. "Surely," she said, "you will give to a man of consular rank some few slaves, from whose hand he may take his food, by whom he may be clothed, by whom he may be shod; all this I alone will provide." She did not obtain it: she hired a little fishing boat, and in that tiny vessel followed the huge ship. The same woman, before Claudius, when the wife of Scribonianus was offering to give evidence, said: "Shall I listen to you, in whose lap Scribonianus was slain, and you live?" From which it is manifest that her resolve of a most noble death was not sudden. Nay more, when Thrasea her son-in-law was begging her not to persist in dying, and among other things had said, "Do you then wish your daughter, if I must perish, to die with me?", she answered: "If she shall have lived with you as long and in as great concord as I with Paetus, I do." By this answer she increased the anxiety of her family; she was watched more attentively; she perceived it, and said: "You do nothing; for you can bring it about that I die ill, that I die not, you cannot." As she said this, she sprang up from her chair and dashed her head against the opposite wall with great force, and fell. Brought round, she said: "I had told you that I would find some way, however hard, to death, if you refused me an easy one." Do not these things seem to you greater than that "Paetus, it does not hurt," to which she came through these? while meanwhile that saying great fame carries about, but these none. Whence it is gathered, as I said at the beginning, that some things are more famous, others greater. Farewell.
17.1. Is all well, since for a long time now your letters have ceased? Or is all well, but you are busy? Or are you not busy, but the occasion of writing is either rare or none?
17.2. Take away this scruple from me, which I cannot bear, take it away even by sending a courier on purpose. I will give the travelling money, I will give even a reward, only let him bring word of what I wish.
17.3. I myself am well, if it is being well to live in suspense and anxiety, expecting from hour to hour and fearing for a most dear friend's life whatever can befall a man. Farewell.
18.1. The duty of the consulship enjoined upon me that, in the name of the state, I should give thanks to the prince. When I had done this in the Senate, having regard, according to custom, to place and time, I thought it most befitting a good citizen to embrace those same things more amply and richly in a volume,
18.2. first that our emperor's virtues might be commended to him by true praises, then that future princes might be forewarned — not as by a teacher, yet by example — by what way above all they might strive to the same glory.
18.3. For to prescribe what a prince ought to be is a fine thing indeed, but burdensome and almost arrogant; but to praise the best of princes, and thereby to show to posterity, as from a watchtower, a light which they may follow, has the same usefulness without any arrogance.
18.4. I took no small pleasure in this, that, when I had wished to recite this book to my friends, they came together, invited not by notes, not by little books, but by "if convenient" and "if very much at leisure" — and at Rome it is never very much at leisure, nor convenient, to hear a reciter — and that too in the foulest weather, for two days; and when my modesty would have made an end of the recitation, they demanded that I add a third day.

title: Letters
text:
18.5. Shall I think this honour paid to me, or to letters? To letters, I prefer; for they, almost extinguished, are being revived.
18.6. But to what subject did they show this assiduity? Surely to one which even in the Senate, where it was necessary to endure it, we were wont to find tiresome even for a moment of time; the same now, men are found who wish both to recite and to hear it for three days — not because it is written more eloquently than before, but because it is written more freely, and therefore also more gladly.
18.7. This too, then, shall be added to the praises of our prince, that a thing before as hateful as it was false has now, being true, become also lovable.
18.8. But I marvellously approved both the zeal of the hearers and their judgment: for I noticed that the severest passages most of all gave satisfaction.
18.9. I remember indeed that I recited to few what I wrote for all; nonetheless, as though the opinion of all would be the same, I rejoice in this severity of ears, and, as once the theatres taught bad musicians to sing ill, so now I am led to hope that it may come about that the same theatres teach musicians to sing well.
18.10. For all who write for the sake of pleasing will write such things as they see please. And for my part I am confident that in this kind of subject the reckoning of a more cheerful style holds good, since those things rather which I wrote more compressedly and tautly, than those which I wrote more gaily and, as it were, more exultantly, may seem far-fetched and forced. Yet not on that account do I pray the less earnestly that some day a day may come — and would it had already come! — when these sweet and winning things may, even by just possession, give place to those austere and severe ones.
