As consul designate, I abstained from all this — if not flattery, yet the appearance of flattery — not as though free and steadfast, but as understanding our prince, whose chief praise I saw to be this, if I decreed nothing as if from necessity.
27.3. I recalled, too, that very many honours had been conferred on every worst man, from whom this best one could be distinguished by nothing more than by a difference in proposing; which very thing I did not pass over by dissimulation and silence, lest perhaps it should seem not my deliberate judgement but forgetfulness.
27.4. This I did then; but the same things do not please all, nor even suit all. Besides, the reason for doing something or not doing it changes with the condition both of the men themselves and of circumstances and times.
27.5. For the recent works of our greatest prince afford the means of proposing things new, great, and true. For which reasons, as I wrote above, I doubt whether I should now advise you the same that then I advised myself. Of this I do not doubt: that I ought to set, as part of your deliberation, what I myself had done. Farewell.
28.1. I know what cause was a hindrance to you, that you could not outstrip my arrival in Campania. But, though absent, you have wholly migrated hither: so great a store, both of city and of country things, has been offered me in your name, all of which, shamelessly, I have nonetheless accepted.
28.2. For your people asked me to do so, and I feared you would be angry both with me and with them, if I had not. In future, unless you all use moderation, I will use it; and I have already given notice to your people that, if they bring so many things again, they will carry all back.
28.3. You will say that I ought to use your things as my own. Granted; but I spare them just as I spare my own. Farewell.
29.1. Avidius Quietus, who loved me singularly and — at which I rejoice no less — approved of me, used often to relate, among many other sayings of Thrasea — for he was his intimate — this one: that he was wont to advise that those causes should be undertaken which were either of friends, or destitute of advocates, or pertaining to a precedent.
29.2. Why those of friends, needs no interpretation. Why those destitute? Because in them above all both the firmness and the humanity of the pleader were seen. Why those pertaining to a precedent? Because it mattered most whether a good or a bad example were introduced.
29.3. To these kinds of causes I will add — ambitiously, perhaps, yet I will add them — the famous and illustrious. For it is fair to plead sometimes for glory and fame, that is, one's own cause. These limits, since you have consulted me, I set for your dignity and modesty.
29.4. Nor does it escape me that practice both is and is held the best teacher of speaking; I see, too, many men of small talent and no letters, who have attained to pleading well by pleading.
29.5. But also that saying, which I have received as Pollio's, or as if Pollio's, I find most true: "By pleading well it came about that I pleaded often, by pleading often that I pleaded less well" — because, of course, by too much assiduity, glibness rather than capacity, and not confidence but rashness, is acquired.

title: Letters
text:
29.6. Nor indeed did it hinder Isocrates from being held a supreme orator, that by weakness of voice and timidity of brow he was prevented from speaking in public. So read much, write, meditate, that you may be able to speak when you wish: you will speak when you must wish.
29.7. This middle course I myself have generally observed; sometimes I have obeyed necessity, which is part of reason. For I have pleaded certain causes by order of the Senate, which yet were, by that division of Thrasea, of the kind pertaining to a precedent.
29.8. I appeared for the Baetici against Baebius Massa: it was asked whether an inquiry should be granted; it was granted. I appeared again for the same men, complaining of Caecilius Classicus: it was asked whether the provincials should be punished as the allies and ministers of the proconsul; they paid the penalty.
29.9. I accused Marius Priscus, who, condemned under the law of extortion, was profiting by the clemency of the law, whose severity he had exceeded by the enormity of his crimes; he was banished.
29.10. I defended Julius Bassus, a man too little guarded and incautious, but by no means bad; judges being granted, he remained in the Senate.
29.11. I pleaded lately for Varenus, who requested that he too be allowed in turn to summon witnesses; it was granted. For the future I wish that I may be ordered above all to do those things which it would befit me to have done even of my own accord. Farewell.
30.1. We ought, by Hercules, to celebrate your birthdays just as we do our own, since the gladness of ours depends upon yours, by whose diligence and care we are cheerful here and carefree there.
30.2. The Camillian villa, which you possess in Campania, is indeed worn by age; and yet, what are the more precious parts, either remain whole or are very slightly damaged.
30.3. We are taking heed, then, that they be repaired as soundly as possible. I seem to have many friends, but of this kind, which both you seek and the matter requires, almost none.
30.4. For they are all of the toga and of the city; but the management of country estates requires some hard and rustic man, to whom neither that labour seems heavy, nor the care sordid, nor the solitude sad.
30.5. You think most honourably of Rufus; for he was an intimate of your son. What, however, he can render us there, I do not know; that he is most willing, I believe. Farewell.
31.1. Summoned into council by our Caesar to Centum Cellae — for this is the name of the place — I took great pleasure.
31.2. For what is more agreeable than to observe the prince's justice, gravity, and courtesy, in his retirement too, where they are most laid open? There were various inquiries, such as might test the judge's virtues through several aspects.
31.3. Claudius Aristion, a leading man of the Ephesians, pleaded his cause — a munificent man and innocently popular; hence envy, and an informer set on by men most unlike him; and so he was acquitted and vindicated.
31.4. On the following day Gallitta was heard, charged with adultery. Married to a military tribune about to seek office, she had stained both her own and her husband's dignity by love of a centurion. The husband had written to the consular legate, the legate to Caesar.
31.5. Caesar, having sifted the proofs, cashiered the centurion and even banished him. There remained, to the crime, which could not be of one alone, the other part of the vengeance; but the husband, not without some reproach for his patience, was held back by love of his wife, whom indeed even after the adultery was reported he had kept at home, as if content to have removed his rival.

title: Letters
text:
31.6. Admonished to carry through the accusation, he carried it through unwillingly. But it was necessary that she be condemned even against the will of her accuser: she was condemned and left to the penalties of the Julian law. Caesar added to the sentence both the name of the centurion and a mention of military discipline, lest he should seem to recall all cases of that kind to himself.
31.7. On the third day was brought in an inquiry tossed about by much talk and varied rumour: the codicil of Julius Tiro, which it was agreed was in part genuine, in part said to be forged.
31.8. As guilty of the crime were named Sempronius Senecio, a Roman knight, and Eurythmus, Caesar's freedman and procurator. The heirs, while Caesar was in Dacia, had jointly written a letter asking that he take up the inquiry.
31.9. He had taken it up; on his return he had appointed a day, and when some of the heirs were dropping the accusation as if out of respect for Eurythmus, he had said most admirably: "He is not Polyclitus, nor am I Nero." Yet he had granted the petitioners a delay, the time of which being now elapsed, he had sat down to hear.
31.10. On the part of the heirs only two came in; they demanded that either all the heirs be compelled to plead, since all had laid the charge, or that to them too leave be given to desist.
31.11. Caesar spoke with the utmost gravity, the utmost moderation; and when the advocate of Senecio and Eurythmus had said that the accused were being left under suspicions unless they were heard, he said: "I do not care whether these men are left under suspicions; I am left under them."
31.12. Then, turning to us: "Consider what we ought to do; for these men wish to complain that it has been permitted them not to accuse." Then, by the council's verdict, he ordered notice given to all the heirs, that either they plead or each one prove his reasons for not pleading; otherwise he would pronounce even on a charge of false accusation.
31.13. You see how honourable, how severe, were the days; which most pleasant relaxations followed. We were invited daily to dinner; it was modest, if you considered him a prince. Sometimes we heard entertainments, sometimes the night was drawn out in most pleasant conversations.
31.14. On the last day, as we were departing — so attentive is the courtesy in Caesar — parting-gifts were sent us. But to me, as the gravity of the inquiries, the honour of the council, the sweetness and frankness of the company, so the place itself was most delightful.
31.15. A most beautiful villa is girdled by greenest fields, and overlooks the shore, in whose bay a harbour is at this very moment being made. The left arm of this is fortified with most solid work; the right is being laboured at.
31.16. In the mouth of the harbour an island rises, which may break the sea, driven in by the wind, that lies before it, and afford a safe passage to ships on either side. It rises, moreover, by an art worth seeing: a very broad vessel brings up huge rocks against it; these, cast down one upon another, hold by their own weight, and are gradually built up into a kind of mound, as it were.
31.17. Already a rocky ridge stands out and shows itself, and dashes the waves driven against it to an immense height and flings them up; there is a vast roar, and the sea is white all around. Then to the rocks piers will be added, which in time to come may imitate an island grown up of itself. This harbour will have, and already has, the name of its founder, and will be most salutary; for along a very long stretch of harbourless coast it will serve as a refuge. Farewell.

title: Letters
text:
32.1. Although you yourself are most temperate, and have brought up your daughter as became your daughter, the granddaughter of Tutilius, yet, since she is about to marry a most honourable man, Nonius Celer, on whom the conduct of public office imposes a certain necessity of splendour, she ought, according to her husband's condition, to use dress and an attendance by which dignity is not indeed increased, yet is adorned and equipped.
32.2. You, moreover, I know to be most blessed in mind, but modest in means. And so I claim part of your burden for myself, and, as a second parent of our girl, I contribute fifty thousand sesterces — meaning to contribute more, did I not trust that it could be obtained from your modesty by the very smallness of the little gift, that you would not refuse it. Farewell.
33.1. "Take away all things," he says, "and put away the labours you have begun!" Whether you are writing or reading something, bid it be taken away, put away, and receive my speech, like those divine arms — could I have been more arrogant? — in truth, as a beautiful one among mine; for it is enough for me to compete with myself.
33.2. This is the speech for Attia Viriola, distinguished both by the rank of the person, by the rarity of the precedent, and by the greatness of the trial. For a woman of splendid birth, married to a man of praetorian rank, disinherited by her octogenarian father within eleven days after he, captured by love, had brought home a stepmother for her, was reclaiming her paternal property in a fourfold trial.
33.3. There sat a hundred and eighty judges — for so many are gathered for the four panels — a great body of advocates on either side and crowded benches; besides, a dense ring of bystanders encircled the very broad court in a manifold circle.
33.4. In addition, the tribunal was thronged, and even from the upper part of the basilica both women and men leaned over, in eagerness both to hear — which was hard — and — which was easy — to see. Great was the expectation of the fathers, great of the daughters, great even of the stepmothers.
33.5. A varied outcome followed; for in two panels we won, in as many we were defeated. Notable indeed and marvellous, in the same case, with the same judges, the same advocates, at the same time, so great a diversity.
33.6. It happened by chance, what might not seem chance: the stepmother was defeated, herself heir to a sixth part; defeated was Suburanus, who, disinherited by his own father, was claiming with singular impudence the property of another's father, not daring to seek his own.
33.7. These things I have set out to you, first that you might know from a letter what you could not from the speech, then — for I will lay bare my arts — that you might read the speech the more gladly, if you seemed not to be reading it but to be present at the trial; which, however great it be, I do not despair of obtaining for it the favour due to the very briefest.
33.8. For it is renewed both by abundance of matter and by acute division and by several little narratives and by variety of expression. There are many things — I should not dare to say it save to you — elevated, many combative, many subtle.
33.9. For there intervened, amid those keen and lofty passages, a frequent necessity of reckoning and almost of calling for counters and a table, so that suddenly the trial before the Court of the Hundred was turned into the form of a private suit.
33.10. We gave the sails to indignation, we gave them to anger, we gave them to grief, and in a most ample cause we were borne, as on a great sea, by many winds.

title: Letters
text:
33.11. In short, certain of my companions are wont to esteem this speech — I will say it again — to be, among mine, my "On the Crown"; whether truly, you will most easily judge, who hold all of them so faithfully in memory that you can compare them with this while you read this one alone. Farewell.
34.1. You did rightly in promising a gladiatorial show to our people of Verona, by whom you have long been loved, respected, honoured. From them too you had a wife most dear to you and most approved, to whose memory either some work or some spectacle, and this above all, which most befits a funeral, was owed.
34.2. Besides, you were asked with so great a consensus that to refuse would have seemed not steadfast but harsh. This also was admirable, that you were so ready, so liberal in giving it; for through these things too a great spirit is shown.
34.3. I could wish that the African beasts, of which you had bought very many, had arrived by the appointed day; but although they were delayed, detained by weather, you nevertheless deserved that it should be credited to you, since it was not through you that you did not exhibit them. Farewell.
1.1. This persistent illness of yours alarms me, and although I know you to be most temperate, I am afraid nevertheless that it may take some liberty even with your character.
1.2. So I urge you to resist it patiently: this is praiseworthy, this is health-giving. Human nature admits the advice I give.
1.3. I myself, at least, when in good health, am accustomed to speak thus to my household: 'I hope, indeed, that if I happen to fall into some adverse illness, I shall desire nothing that would deserve either shame or regret; but if the disease should prove too strong, I give notice that you are to give me nothing except what the doctors permit, and you may be sure that if you do give it, I shall take my revenge as others do over what is refused them.'
1.4. Indeed, when I was burning with a most violent fever, and at last, the fever having eased and I having been anointed, was about to take a draught from the doctor, I held out my hand and told him to touch it, and gave back the cup when it had already been brought to my lips.
1.5. Afterwards, when on the twentieth day of my illness I was being prepared for the bath and suddenly saw the doctors whispering together, I asked the reason. They answered that I could bathe safely, yet not altogether without some risk.
1.6. 'What need is there of it?' I said; and so, calmly and gently giving up the hope of the bath, to which I already seemed to be carried, I composed my mind and my expression for abstinence again, just as I had a moment before for the bath.
1.7. I have written this to you, first to admonish you not without an example, and then so that for the future I might bind myself to the same temperance, having pledged myself by this letter as by a kind of bond. Farewell.
2.1. How does it agree, that you should both assert you are hindered by ceaseless engagements, and yet long for my writings, which can scarcely win any of their fleeting time even from men of leisure?
2.2. I shall let the summer pass, then, restless and busy for you, and only in winter, when it will be credible that you can be free at least during the nights, shall I look out which of my trifles I had best offer you.
2.3. Meanwhile it is more than enough if my letters are not a burden; but they are, and so they shall be the shorter. Farewell.
3.1. With such persistence are you now in Lucania, now in Campania? 'For I myself,' you say, 'am Lucanian, my wife Campanian.'

title: Letters
text:
3.2. A fair reason for a longer absence, but not a perpetual one. Why, then, do you not at some time return to the city? Here are rank, office, friendships both with your superiors and with your inferiors. How long will you reign? How long will you stay awake when you please, sleep as long as you please? How long will your shoes lie unused, your toga on holiday, the whole day free?
3.3. It is time you revisited our annoyances, if only for this reason, that those pleasures of yours may not grow stale through surfeit. Pay your respects for a while, so that being paid respects may be more agreeable to you; wear yourself out in this crowd, so that solitude may delight you.
3.4. But why, foolishly, do I hold back one whom I am trying to summon? For perhaps by these very words you are reminded to wrap yourself more and more in leisure — which I do not wish to be broken off, but only interrupted.
3.5. For just as, if I were preparing a dinner for you, I should mix sharp and pungent dishes with the sweet ones, so that the palate, dulled and cloyed by the former, might be roused by the latter, so now I urge you to season that most agreeable manner of life from time to time with a few sour touches, as it were. Farewell.
4.1. You say you have read my hendecasyllables; you ask, too, how I came to write them — I, a man you think severe, and one not, by my own confession, inept.
4.2. I have never — to go back further — been a stranger to poetry; indeed, at the age of fourteen I wrote a Greek tragedy. 'Of what kind?' you ask. I do not know; it was called a tragedy.
4.3. Later, when returning from military service I was detained by the winds on the island of Icaria, I composed Latin elegiacs on that very sea and island. I once tried my hand at heroic verse too, and now for the first time at hendecasyllables, whose birth had this occasion. There were being read to me at my Laurentine villa the books of Asinius Gallus comparing his father and Cicero. A certain epigram of Cicero's to his freedman Tiro turned up.
4.4. Then, when at midday — for it was summer — I had withdrawn to sleep, and sleep would not come, I began to reflect that the greatest orators had held this kind of pursuit among their delights and reckoned it among their glories.
4.5. I set my mind to it, and contrary to my own expectation, after a long disuse, in a very brief span of time I scratched out in these verses the very matter that had prompted me to write:
4.6. When I was reading Gallus' books, in which he dared
to award his own father palm and honour above Cicero,
I found a playful jest of Cicero's, to be admired
for that same genius with which he composed his serious works, and with which,
by human wit and much and varied charm,
he showed that the minds of great men take delight.
For he complains that, cheated by a wicked trick of his loving heart,
Tiro after dinner withheld from him in the night
the few little kisses that were his due.
4.5b. When I had read this,
'Why after this,' I said, 'do we conceal our own loves,
and timidly bring nothing forward, nor confess
Tiro's wiles, and admit we know Tiro's fugitive
endearments and his thefts that add new flames?'
4.7. I passed on to elegiacs; these too I unfolded no less swiftly, and added others, led astray by the ease of it. Then, returning to the city, I read them to my companions; they approved.
4.8. After that, whenever I had leisure, and especially on a journey, I tried more metres. At last I resolved, after the example of many, to finish off one separate volume of hendecasyllables by itself, and I do not regret it.

title: Letters
text:
4.9. It is read, copied out, even sung — and by Greeks too, whom love of this little book has taught Latin — now to the cithara, now to the lyre.
4.10. But why so boastfully? Though poets are allowed to be mad. And yet I speak not of my own judgement but of others'; and whether they judge rightly or err, it delights me. One thing only I pray: that posterity may either err in the same way or judge as they do. Farewell.
5.1. It is incredible with what longing for you I am held. The cause is, first, love, and then that we are not used to being apart. Hence it is that I spend a great part of the nights awake with your image before me; hence that in the daytime, at the hours when I used to visit you, my own feet carry me — as the saying truly goes — to your apartment; and then, sick and sorrowful and like one shut out, I withdraw from the empty threshold. The one time free from these torments is when I am worn down in the forum by my friends' lawsuits.
5.2. Judge for yourself what my life is, when my rest lies in toil, my solace in misery and cares. Farewell.
6.1. A rare and remarkable thing has befallen Varenus, though it is still uncertain. The Bithynians are said to have dropped their accusation against him as rashly begun. 'Said,' do I call it? The province's envoy is here; he has brought the council's decree to the Emperor, brought it to many leading men, brought it even to us, Varenus' advocates.
6.2. Yet that same Magnus persists; indeed, he presses Nigrinus, an excellent man, most obstinately. Through him he was demanding of the consuls that Varenus be compelled to produce his accounts.
6.3. I was assisting Varenus now only as a friend, and had resolved to keep silent. For nothing would be more contrary than that, an advocate assigned by the Senate, I should defend as guilty one who needed not to seem guilty at all.
6.4. When, however, Nigrinus' demand being finished, the consuls turned their eyes on me, I said: 'You shall learn that the reason for our silence is consistent, when you have heard the true envoys of the province.' Nigrinus countered: 'To whom were they sent?' I: 'To me as well: I have the province's decree.'
6.5. Again he: 'It may be clear to you.' To this I: 'If it is clear to you from the other side, it can also be clear to me, on the better side.'
6.6. Then the envoy Polyaenus set out the reasons for the abandoned accusation, and demanded that no prejudgement be made of the Emperor's cognizance. Magnus replied, and Polyaenus again. I myself, intervening rarely and briefly, kept much within silence.
6.7. For I have learned that at times it is no less the part of an orator to be silent than to speak. And indeed I recall that with certain defendants on capital charges I have done more good by silence than by the most careful speech.
6.8. A mother, having lost her son — for what forbids me, though the letter was begun for another reason, to discourse on matters of study? — had accused his freedmen, who were also her co-heirs, of forgery and poisoning before the Emperor, and had obtained Julius Servianus as judge.
6.9. I had defended the accused before a huge gathering; for the case was very well known, and besides, on both sides there were the most distinguished talents. The question was settled by an examination under torture, which decided in the defendants' favour.
6.10. Afterwards the mother went to the Emperor and affirmed she had found new proofs. Suburanus was instructed to give a hearing to one reopening a concluded case, if she should bring anything new.

title: Letters
text:
6.11. Julius Africanus, grandson of that orator at whose word Passienus Crispus once said, 'Well, by Hercules, well — but to what purpose so well?', was assisting the mother. The grandson of this man, a clever young fellow but not a little crafty, when he had said much and filled out his allotted time, said: 'I ask, Suburanus, that you permit me to add one word.'
6.12. Then I, when all were looking at me as though I should reply at length, said: 'I would have replied, had Africanus added that one word, in which I do not doubt that everything would have been new.'
6.13. I cannot easily recall ever winning by pleading as much approval as I then won by not pleading. In like manner now both my silence on behalf of Varenus, so far, has been approved and well received.
6.14. The consuls, as Polyaenus had demanded, reserved everything intact for the Emperor; whose hearing I await in suspense. For that day will give us, on Varenus' behalf, either security and rest, or, with our interrupted labour renewed, lay fresh anxiety upon us. Farewell.
7.1. I have thanked our friend Priscus both recently and again now, because you bade me. Most gladly, indeed: for it is very pleasant to me that two excellent men, both my very dear friends, have grown so close to each other that you each think yourselves obligated to the other.
7.2. For he too declares that he derives a particular pleasure from your friendship, and competes with you in a most honourable contest of mutual affection, which time itself will increase. That you are detained by business I take amiss only because you cannot devote yourself to your studies. Yet if you will settle one suit through a judge and the other — as you say — yourself, you will first begin to enjoy leisure there, then, having had your fill, return to us. Farewell.
8.1. I cannot express how pleasant it is to me that our friend Saturninus, in letter after letter, renders you the warmest thanks in my hearing.
8.2. Go on as you have begun, and love this most excellent man as intimately as possible, since you will derive great pleasure from his friendship, and that for no brief time.
8.3. For while he abounds in all virtues, he excels above all in this, that he has the greatest steadfastness in friendship. Farewell.
9.1. You ask how I think you ought to study in the retirement you have now long been enjoying.
9.2. Useful above all — and many recommend it — is to translate either from Greek into Latin or from Latin into Greek. By this kind of exercise one acquires precision and brilliance of words, a wealth of figures, force of exposition, and, besides, the faculty of inventing what is similar to the best by imitating them; at the same time, what would have escaped a reader cannot escape a translator.
9.3. From this one acquires understanding and judgement. It will do no harm, when you have read a passage far enough to grasp its subject and argument, to write something as a rival to it, and then to compare it with what you have read, and carefully to weigh which is better, yours or his. Great is your satisfaction if some things of yours are better, great your shame if everything of his is. You may sometimes choose even the most famous passages and compete with what you have chosen.
9.4. This is bold, yet not presumptuous, because it is a private contest: though we see many who have taken up such contests for themselves with much praise, and have outstripped those whom they had thought it enough merely to follow, so long as they did not despair.

title: Letters
text:
9.5. You may also revise what you have spoken, after it has faded from memory; retain much, pass over more, rewrite some parts, recast others.
9.6. This is laborious and full of tedium, but for that very difficulty fruitful: to grow warm again from the beginning and resume an impulse once broken and abandoned; and finally to weave new limbs, as it were, into a finished body without disturbing the earlier ones.
9.7. I know that your chief study now is oratory; but I would not on that account always recommend this combative and, as it were, warlike style. For just as the earth is renewed by various and changing seeds, so are our minds refreshed by now this practice, now that.
9.8. I would have you sometimes take up a passage from history; I would have you write a letter more carefully. For often in oratory too there arises a need for descriptions not merely historical but almost poetic, while a terse and pure manner of speech is to be drawn from letters.
9.9. It is permissible also to relax with verse — I do not mean continuous and long verse, for that cannot be accomplished except in leisure, but this pointed and brief kind, which fittingly breaks up any amount of business and care.
9.10. They are called trifles; but these trifles sometimes win no less glory than serious works. And indeed — for why should I not exhort you to verse in verse? —
9.11. as it is the merit of wax to follow, soft and yielding,
the skilled fingers, and at command to become the work bidden,
now to shape Mars or chaste Minerva,
now to fashion Venus, now Venus' boy;
and as sacred springs not only quench fires
but often delight too with flowers and spring meadows,
so it befits the mind of men to be bent and led through arts
not rigid, with a trained agility.
9.12. And so the greatest orators, the greatest men too, used either to exercise or to delight themselves in this way — rather, to delight and exercise themselves at once.
9.13. For it is wonderful how the mind is both strained and relaxed by these little works. They take in love and hatred, anger and pity, urbanity — everything, in short, that has its place in life and even in the forum and the courts.
9.14. In these too there is the same usefulness as in other verse: that, bound by the necessity of metre, we rejoice in unfettered prose, and that, since comparison shows it to be easier, we write the more willingly.
9.15. You have here perhaps even more than you asked for; yet one thing I have omitted. For I have not said what I think should be read — though I have said it, when I said what should be written. Remember to choose carefully the authors in each kind. For they say much should be read, not many things.
9.16. Who these authors are is so well known and approved that it needs no pointing out; and besides, I have drawn this letter out so immoderately that, while advising you how you ought to study, I have taken away the time for studying. Why then do you not take up your tablets again and write something, either one of these things or that very piece you had begun? Farewell.
10.1. Because I myself, when I have learned the first part of a matter, am eager to join the last to it, I suppose that you too wish to learn the rest about Varenus and the Bithynians. The case was argued, on one side by Polyaenus, on the other by Magnus.
10.2. When the pleadings were finished, the Emperor said: 'Neither party shall complain of delay; it will be my concern to discover the province's will.'
10.3. Meanwhile Varenus gained much. For how doubtful is it whether a man is justly accused, when it is uncertain whether he is accused at all! It remains only that the province may not approve again what it is said to have condemned, and repent of its own repentance. Farewell.

title: Letters
text:
11.1. You wonder that my freedman Hermes, without waiting for the auction, made over my fifth share of the inherited lands — which I had ordered to be advertised — to Corellia for seven hundred thousand sesterces. You add that these could fetch nine hundred thousand, and so all the more you ask whether I uphold what he has done.
11.2. Indeed I uphold it; for what reasons, hear. For I wish it to be both approved by you and excused by my co-heirs, that, at the bidding of a greater duty, I set myself apart from them.
11.3. I love and revere Corellia with the greatest respect, first as the sister of Corellius Rufus, whose memory is sacred to me, and then as the closest friend of my mother.
11.4. I have old ties too with her husband Minicius Justus, an excellent man; and I had the greatest with her son, so much so that he presided over the games I gave as praetor.
11.5. When I was last there, she let me know that she desired to own something around our Lake Como. I offered her, out of my own estates, whatever she wished and at whatever price she wished — except those that came from my mother and father; for these I cannot yield even to Corellia.
11.6. So when this inheritance fell to me, in which those properties were included, I wrote to her that they would be for sale. Hermes carried these letters, and when she demanded that he should make over my share to her at once, he obeyed. You see how bound I am to ratify what my freedman has done in accordance with my own principles.
11.7. It remains that my co-heirs should bear with an even mind my having sold separately what I might have not sold at all.
11.8. Nor indeed are they compelled to imitate my example: for they have not the same ties with Corellia as I have. They may therefore look to their own interest, in place of which I had friendship. Farewell.
12.1. The little book I composed, as you had required, so that your friend — or rather ours, for what is not common to us? — might use it if the case should call for it, I have sent you the more slowly so that you might not have time to correct it, that is, to spoil it.
12.2. Yet you shall have time — to correct it I know not, but at any rate to spoil it. For you over-zealous people draw off all the best parts.
12.3. But if you do so, I shall take it in good part. For afterwards I shall use those very passages as my own on some occasion, and by the benefit of your fastidiousness I myself shall be praised — as in that passage which you will find I have marked, and explained otherwise in a note above.
12.4. For when I suspected that it would seem to you too inflated, since it is more sonorous and lofty, I thought it not amiss, lest you should torment yourself, to add at once something more compressed and slender, or rather more lowly and worse, yet by your judgement more correct.
12.5. For why should I not everywhere pursue and harry your thinness of style? This, that you might sometimes laugh a little amid those engagements of yours; that other matter in earnest:
12.6. see that you repay me the travelling expense which I incurred deliberately by dispatching a courier. Surely, when you read this, you will condemn not parts of the little book but the whole book, and deny that anything is of any value the price of which is demanded back from you. Farewell.
13.1. The same letter signifies both that you are not studying and that you are. Do I speak in riddles? Quite plainly, until I declare more distinctly what I mean.
13.2. For it denies that you are studying, yet it is so polished that it cannot have been written except by one who studies; or else you are blessed above all men, if you accomplish such things in idleness and leisure. Farewell.

title: Letters
text:
14.1. You act most honourably in asking and insisting so earnestly that I should order the price of the lands to be accepted from you not at the seven hundred thousand for which you bought them from my freedman, but at the nine hundred thousand for which you bought the twentieth part from the tax-farmers.
14.2. In my turn I both ask and insist that you look not only to what becomes you but also to what becomes me, and that you allow me to resist you in this one thing with the same spirit with which I am accustomed to comply with you in all. Farewell.
15.1. You ask what I am doing. What you know: I am torn by my duties, I serve my friends, I study now and then — which to do not now and then but only and always would have been, I dare not say more rightly, but certainly more blessedly.
15.2. I should be vexed that you are doing anything other than what you wish, were not the things you are doing most honourable. For both to manage the affairs of one's community and to arbitrate among friends is most deserving of praise.
15.3. I knew that the company of our friend Priscus would be pleasant to you. I had known his openness, I had known his courtesy; and that he is also — what I had known less — most grateful, I find by experience, since you write that he so pleasantly remembers our good offices. Farewell.
16.1. I love Calestrius Tiro most intimately, bound to me by ties both private and public.
16.2. We served together in the army, were together quaestors of the Emperor. He preceded me in the tribunate by virtue of the right of three children; I overtook him in the praetorship, when the Emperor remitted a year for me. I have often retired to his villas, he has often recovered his health in my house.
16.3. He is now about to make for the province of Baetica as proconsul, by way of Ticinum.
16.4. I hope — rather, I am confident — that I shall easily obtain that he turn aside from his route to you, if you wish to free by formal manumission those whom you lately set free among your friends. There is no reason for you to fear that this may be a trouble to him, for whom it will not be far to go round the whole world for my sake.
16.5. So lay aside that excessive bashfulness of yours, and consult what you wish. To him what I bid will be as pleasant as to me what you bid. Farewell.
17.1. Each man has his own reason for reciting; mine, as I have often said, is that if anything escapes me — as it certainly does — I may be reminded of it.
17.2. So I wonder all the more that, as you write, there have been some who found fault that I recited speeches at all; unless indeed they think that these alone need no correction.
17.3. Of these men I would gladly ask why they grant — if indeed they grant it — that history ought to be recited, which is composed not for display but for faith and truth; why tragedy, which calls not for an audience-hall but for a stage and actors; why lyric, which demands not a reader but a chorus and a lyre. Yet the recitation of these is now established by custom.
17.4. Is the man who began it, then, to be blamed? Though speeches too have been read aloud both by certain of our own people and by the Greeks.
17.5. Still, it is superfluous to recite what you have already delivered. Yes — if you recite the whole, the same, to the same persons, immediately; but if you insert much, change much, take on some new hearers and some of the same but after an interval, why is the reason for reciting what you have delivered less commendable than for publishing it?

title: Letters
text:
17.6. But it is difficult for a speech to satisfy while it is being recited. That, however, belongs to the labour of the reciter, not to any reason for not reciting.
17.7. And in truth I desire to be praised not while I recite but while I am read. And so I omit no kind of correction. First I go over by myself what I have written; then I read it to two or three; next I hand it to others for annotation, and their notes, if I am in doubt, I weigh again with one or another; last of all I recite it to several, and then, if you believe me at all, I correct most keenly;
17.8. for the more anxiously, the more diligently I attend. The reverence, the shame, the fear of an audience are the best of all judges — and consider it thus: if you are going to speak with someone, however learned, but one only, are you not less moved than if with many, even unlearned?
17.9. When you rise to plead, do you not then most of all distrust yourself, then desire to change not, I say, most things, but everything? — especially if the stage is broader and the surrounding circle wider; for we hold in awe even those mean and shabbily clad ones.
17.10. If you think that your very first words are disapproved, are you not weakened and undone? I suppose because in number itself there is a kind of great and combined judgement, and those who singly have little discernment have most of all together.
17.11. And so Pomponius Secundus — that writer of tragedies — when some passage that a more intimate friend thought should be removed, but he himself thought should be kept, was at issue, used to say: 'I appeal to the people'; and thus, from the people's silence or assent, he followed either his own opinion or his friend's.
17.12. So much did he yield to the people; rightly or not is nothing to me. For I am accustomed to call in not the people but a chosen and select few, on whom I may keep my eyes, whom I may trust, whom in short I may both observe as individuals and fear as not individuals.
17.13. For what Marcus Cicero felt about the pen, I feel about fear: fear is the keenest of correctors. The very thought that we are about to recite corrects us; entering the audience-hall corrects us; that we grow pale, shudder, and look about us corrects us.
17.14. So I do not regret a habit which I find most useful, and so far from being deterred by the chatter of those men, I even ask you of my own accord to point out something I may add to my methods.
17.15. For nothing is enough for my care. I consider how great a thing it is to put something into men's hands, and I cannot persuade myself that what you wish to please both always and everybody is not to be handled both with many and often. Farewell.
18.1. You consult me how the money which you have offered our townsmen for a public feast may remain safe even after you are gone. An honourable question, but no easy answer. Should you pay over the sum to the community? It is to be feared lest it be frittered away. Should you give lands? As public property they will be neglected.
18.2. For my part I find nothing more convenient than what I myself did. For in place of the five hundred thousand sesterces which I had promised for the maintenance of freeborn boys and girls, I conveyed to a public agent a farm of mine worth far more; the same farm I took back subject to a rent, undertaking to pay thirty thousand a year.
18.3. By this means both the community's capital is safe and its income certain, and the land itself, because the rent largely exceeds it, will always find an owner to work it.

title: Letters
text:
18.4. Nor am I unaware that I have laid out somewhat more than I appear to have given, since the necessity of the rent has reduced the price of a most beautiful estate.
18.5. But one ought to set public advantages before private, eternal before mortal, and to provide for one's gift far more carefully than for one's means. Farewell.
19.1. Fannia's illness distresses me. She contracted it while attending the Vestal virgin Junia — first of her own accord, for she is a relative, then also by the authority of the pontiffs.
19.2. For when the virgins are compelled by the violence of disease to leave the hall of Vesta, they are entrusted to the care and keeping of matrons. While Fannia was diligently discharging this office, she became involved in the present danger.
19.3. Fevers cling to her, her cough increases; she is wasted to the utmost, exhausted to the utmost. Only her mind and spirit are strong, most worthy of her husband Helvidius, of her father Thrasea; all else gives way, and they fill me not with fear only but also with grief.
19.4. For I grieve that a most great woman is being snatched from the eyes of the state, which I do not know whether it will ever see anything like her again. What purity she had, what holiness, what dignity, what steadfastness! Twice she followed her husband into exile; a third time she herself was banished on her husband's account.
19.5. For when Senecio was on trial for having composed books on the life of Helvidius, and had said in his defence that he had been asked by Fannia, and when Mettius Carus asked threateningly whether she had asked him, she answered: 'I asked'; whether she had given him notebooks to write from: 'I gave'; whether with her mother's knowledge: 'Without her knowledge'; in short, she uttered no word that yielded to danger.
19.6. Indeed, those very books, though abolished by a decree of the Senate out of the necessity and fear of the times, she preserved and kept when her property was confiscated, and carried into exile the very cause of her exile.
19.7. The same woman, how agreeable, how courteous, how — what is granted to few — no less lovable than venerable! Will there be one whom we can hereafter hold up as a model to our wives? Will there be one from whom even men may take examples of fortitude, whom, beholding and hearing, we may so admire as those women of whom we read?
19.8. And to me the very house seems to totter and, wrenched from its foundations, to be about to fall upon us, though it still has descendants. For by what great virtues, by what great deeds will they bring it about that she did not perish as the last of her line?
19.9. This too afflicts and tortures me, that her mother — that mother of so great a woman, than whom I can say nothing more illustrious — I seem to lose again, whom this woman, as she gives her back and restores her to us, so will take away with her, and afflict me with a wound at once new and reopened.
19.10. Both I cherished, both I loved: which the more, I do not know, nor did they wish it to be distinguished. They had my services in prosperity, they had them in adversity. I was the comfort of them when banished, the avenger of them when restored; yet I did not repay them in full, and so all the more I desire that this one be preserved, that time may remain for me to discharge my debt.
19.11. In such cares was I when I wrote to you; if some god turns them into joy, I shall not complain of my fear. Farewell.
20.1. I have read your book, and as carefully as I could noted what I thought should be changed, what should be cut out. For I am used to telling the truth, and you to hearing it gladly. Indeed, none are reproached more patiently than those who most deserve to be praised.

title: Letters
text:
20.2. Now I await my book from you with your notes. O pleasant, O lovely exchange! How it delights me that, if posterity has any care for us, it will be told everywhere with what harmony, simplicity, and faith we lived!
20.3. It will be a rare and signal thing that two men, almost equal in age and rank, of some name in literature — for I am forced to speak more sparingly of you too, because I speak of myself at the same time — should each have fostered the other's studies.
20.4. For my part, as a very young man, when you were already flourishing in fame and glory, I longed to follow you, to be and to be reckoned 'next, but at a long interval' behind you. And there were many most distinguished talents; but you seemed to me — so did the kinship of our natures bear it — most able and most fit to be imitated.
20.5. So I rejoice all the more that, if there is any talk of literature, we are named together, that I come at once to the minds of those speaking of you. Nor are there lacking those who are preferred to us both.
20.6. But we — it matters nothing to me in what place — are joined together; for in my eyes the first is he who is nearest you. Indeed, you must have noticed in wills too: unless someone happens to be a special friend of one or the other of us, we receive the same legacies, and that equally.
20.7. All of which looks to this, that we should love each other the more ardently, since so many bonds bind us together — our studies, our characters, our reputation, and finally men's last judgements. Farewell.
21.1. I obey, dearest colleague, and consult my weak eyes as you bid. For I came here shut in on all sides in a covered carriage, as if in a bedroom, and here I refrain — with difficulty — not only from the pen but also from reading, and study with my ears alone.
21.2. I make my bedrooms shady by drawn curtains, yet not dark. The covered colonnade too, with the lower windows closed, has as much shadow as light. Thus little by little I learn to bear the light.
21.3. I take a bath because it does good, wine because it does no harm — most sparingly, however. So I have grown used to it, and now a guardian is at hand.
21.4. The hen, as sent by you, I received gladly; and with eyes sharp enough, though still bleary, I saw it to be very plump. Farewell.
22.1. You will wonder less that I asked so insistently for you to confer a tribunate on my friend, when you learn who and what kind of man he is. I can now both tell you his name and describe the man himself, since you have promised.
22.2. He is Cornelius Minicianus, an ornament of my region whether in rank or in character. Born of high family, he abounds in wealth, yet loves study as the poor are wont to. He is besides a most upright judge, a most courageous advocate, a most faithful friend.
22.3. You will believe you have received a benefit, when you have looked more closely at a man equal to all honours, all titles — I will say nothing too lofty of so modest a man. Farewell.
23.1. I rejoice indeed that you are so vigorous that you can meet Tiro at Mediolanum; but, that you may continue to be so vigorous, I beg you not to lay upon yourself so much toil against the reason of your age. Indeed, I give notice that you are to wait for him both at home and within your house, and even within the threshold of your bedroom.
23.2. For since I love him as a brother, he ought not to demand from one whom I respect in a parent's place an office that he would have excused his own parent. Farewell.
24.1. Ummidia Quadratilla died a little short of her eightieth year, vigorous to her very last illness, and indeed beyond a matron's measure of compact and robust body.

title: Letters
text:
24.2. She died with a most honourable will: she left her grandson heir to two-thirds, her granddaughter to a third. The granddaughter I scarcely know; the grandson I love most intimately, a young man remarkable, and to be loved among his kin not only by those whom he touches by blood.
24.3. And first, conspicuous for his beauty, he passed both boyhood and youth free of all the slanderers' talk; a husband before his twenty-fourth year, and a father too, had the god granted it. He lived in the household of his pleasure-loving grandmother most strictly, and yet most dutifully.
24.4. She kept pantomimes and favoured them more lavishly than befits a woman of rank. These Quadratus would watch neither in the theatre nor at home, nor did she require it.
24.5. I heard from her own lips, when she was commending her grandson's studies to me, that she — as a woman with that leisure of her sex — was accustomed to relax her mind with the play of draughts, and to watch her own pantomimes, but that whenever she was about to do either, she always bade her grandson go away and study; which she seemed to me to do not more from love of him than from respect for him.
24.6. You will wonder — and I wondered too. At the last sacerdotal games, the pantomimes having been brought on at the opening, when Quadratus and I were leaving the theatre together, he said to me: 'Do you know that today, for the first time, I have seen my grandmother's freedman dance?' So said the grandson.
24.7. But, by Hercules, men who were no kin at all kept running to the theatre in Quadratilla's honour — I am ashamed to have said 'honour' — through a service of flattery, leaping, applauding, marvelling, and then giving back each of the lady's gestures with the songs; men who now will receive the tiniest legacies, the perquisite of theatrical service, from the heir who was not even watching.
24.8. This, because you are wont, if anything new occurs, to hear it not unwillingly; and then because it is pleasant to me to go over again in writing the joy I had felt. For I rejoice in the dead woman's devotion, in the honour shown to the excellent young man; I am glad too that the house that once belonged to Gaius Cassius — that founder and head of the Cassian school — will now serve a master no less great.
24.9. For my friend Quadratus will fill it and grace it, and restore to it its former dignity, fame, and glory, since as great an orator will come forth from it as that man was a jurist. Farewell.
25.1. O how much of the learned does either their own modesty or their quiet conceal and withdraw from fame! Yet we fear only those who are about to say or read something — namely, who put forth their studies — whereas those who keep silent give this further proof, that they revere with silence their greatest work.
25.2. I write what I write from experience. Terentius Junior, having most honourably discharged the equestrian military offices and even the procuratorship of the province of Narbonensis, withdrew to his fields, and, with honours ready to hand, preferred the most tranquil leisure.
25.3. Invited to his hospitality, I regarded him as a good head of a household, as a diligent farmer, intending to talk of those matters in which I thought him engaged; and I had begun, when he recalled me to literature with most learned discourse.
25.4. How polished was it all, how Latin, how Greek! For he is so strong in either tongue that he seems to excel rather in the one which he happens to be speaking. How much the man reads, how much he retains! You would think he lived at Athens, not in a country house.

title: Letters
text:
25.5. In short, he increased my anxiety and brought it about that I fear those secluded and, as it were, rustic men no less than those whom I know to be most learned.
25.6. The same I advise you: for as in camps, so in our literary world too, there are, you will find on careful search, more in peasant garb whom you will discover to be girt and armed, and that with the most ardent genius. Farewell.
26.1. The illness of a certain friend lately reminded me that we are at our best when we are ailing. For what sick man is troubled by greed or lust?
26.2. He is not a slave to love-affairs, does not seek honours, neglects wealth, and however little he has, since he is about to leave it, holds it enough. Then he remembers that there are gods, that he himself is a man; he envies no one, admires no one, despises no one; he neither heeds nor is fed by malicious talk: he imagines baths and springs.
26.3. These are the sum of his cares, the sum of his prayers; and he resolves on a life soft and easy for the future, should he chance to escape — that is, a life harmless and blessed.
26.4. So I can, in brief, prescribe for you and for myself what philosophers try to teach in very many words, even in very many volumes: that we persevere in being, while well, such as we profess we shall be while ailing. Farewell.
27.1. Leisure affords me the means of learning and you of teaching. So I very much wish to know whether you think there are phantoms, and that they have a shape of their own and some divine power, or that, empty and unreal, they take on an image from our fear.
27.2. What chiefly leads me to believe they exist is what I hear befell Curtius Rufus. While still of slender means and obscure, he had attached himself as a companion to the governor of Africa. As the day was declining, he was walking in a colonnade; there was offered to him the figure of a woman greater and more beautiful than human. To him in his terror she said she was the foreteller of the future: he would go to Rome and hold offices, and even return to that same province with supreme command, and there die.
27.3. All came to pass. Moreover, it is told that as he approached Carthage and was disembarking, the same figure met him on the shore. He himself, certainly, when seized by illness, augured the future from the past, adversity from prosperity, and gave up hope of recovery though none of his people despaired.
27.4. Now is not this both more terrible and no less wonderful which I shall set forth as I received it?
27.5. There was at Athens a spacious and roomy house, but of ill repute and pestilential. Through the silence of the night a sound of iron, and, if you listened more keenly, a clanking of chains, was returned, far off at first, then close at hand: presently there appeared a spectre, an old man, worn with leanness and squalor, his beard flowing, his hair bristling; on his legs he bore fetters, on his hands chains, and shook them.
27.6. Thence the dwellers passed sad and dreadful nights awake through fear; sickness followed the waking, and, as the dread grew, death. For in the daytime too, though the apparition had withdrawn, the memory of it hovered before their eyes, and the fear lasted longer than its causes. So the house was deserted, condemned to solitude, and left wholly to that monster; yet it was advertised, in case anyone, ignorant of so great an evil, should wish to buy or rent it.
27.7. To Athens came the philosopher Athenodorus; he read the notice, and on hearing the price, because its cheapness was suspect, made inquiry and learned everything; and none the less — rather, all the more — he rented it. When evening began to come on, he ordered a couch to be spread for him in the front part of the house, called for his tablets, a pen, a lamp, and sent all his people into the inner rooms. He himself fixed his mind, eyes, and hand on writing, lest an empty mind should fashion for itself the spectres it had heard of and idle fears.

title: Letters
text:
27.8. At first, the silence of night as everywhere; then the iron was shaken, the chains moved. He did not raise his eyes or lay down his pen, but steadied his mind and shut his ears against the sound. Then the din grew, approached, and now was heard as if on the threshold, now as if within it. He looked round, saw and recognized the figure that had been described to him.
27.9. It stood and beckoned with its finger, as one calling. He on his side signed with his hand that it should wait a little, and bent again over his wax and pen. It clashed its chains over the head of him as he wrote. He looked round again at the same figure beckoning as before, and without delay took up the lamp and followed.
27.10. It went with slow step, as if heavy with its chains. After it had turned aside into the courtyard of the house, it suddenly vanished and deserted its companion. Left alone, he set plucked grass and leaves as a mark of the place.
27.11. The next day he went to the magistrates and urged them to order that place to be dug up. There were found bones entwined and bound with chains, which the body, rotted by time and the earth, had left bare and corroded within the fetters; they were gathered and given public burial. Afterwards the house, the shade having been duly laid to rest, was free of it.
27.12. And these things I believe on the word of those who affirm them; this I can affirm to others. I have a freedman not without education. With him his younger brother used to sleep in the same bed. He seemed to himself to see someone sitting on the couch and bringing scissors to his head, and even cutting off the hair from the very crown. When day came, he was found shorn about the crown, and his hair lying scattered.
27.13. A short interval, and again another like the former gave it credence. A slave-boy was sleeping among many in the boys' quarters. There came — so he tells — through the windows two men in white tunics, who sheared him as he lay and withdrew the way they had come. Him too day showed shorn, with his hair scattered about.
27.14. Nothing notable followed, unless perhaps that I was not accused, though I should have been, had Domitian, under whom these things happened, lived longer. For in his desk was found a paper given against me by Carus; from which it may be conjectured that, since it is the custom for the accused to let their hair grow long, the cutting off of my people's hair was a sign of the danger that threatened me, and that it was averted.
27.15. So I ask you to apply your learning. The matter is worthy of your long and deep consideration; nor am I unworthy that you should bestow on me the abundance of your knowledge.
27.16. You may even argue both sides — as you are wont — yet more strongly on one, so that you do not dismiss me in suspense and uncertainty, when the very cause of my consulting you has been that I might cease to doubt. Farewell.
28.1. You say some at your place have found fault with me, as though I praise my friends beyond measure on every occasion.
28.2. I acknowledge the charge, I even embrace it. For what is more honourable than the fault of kindliness? Yet who are these who know my friends better than I? But, suppose they do know them, why do they grudge me my most happy error? For though they be not such as I proclaim them, still I am blessed because they seem so to me.
28.3. Let them turn this sinister diligence, then, upon others; nor are there few who call carping at their friends judgement. They will never persuade me that I think mine too much loved by me. Farewell.

title: Letters
text:
29.1. You will laugh, then be indignant, then laugh again, if you read this — which, unless you read it, you cannot believe.
29.2. There is, on the Tiburtine way within the first milestone — I noted it lately — a monument of Pallas inscribed thus: 'To him the Senate, for his loyalty and devotion towards his patrons, decreed the praetorian insignia and fifteen million sesterces, with the honour of which he was content.'
29.3. For my part I have never wondered at things that proceed more often from fortune than from judgement; but this inscription above all reminded me how mocking and absurd were the things sometimes flung down into this mire, into these dregs — things which that gallows-bird both dared to accept and to refuse, and even to hand down to posterity as a model of moderation.
29.4. But why am I indignant? Better to laugh, lest those think they have attained something great who come to such a pitch of good fortune as to be laughed at. Farewell.
30.1. I am tormented that you have lost, as you write, a pupil of the highest promise. That your studies should be hindered by his illness and death — why should I not know it? — when you are most observant of all your duties, and love most warmly all whom you approve.
30.2. Here too the city's business pursues me; for there are those who make me a judge or arbiter.
30.3. Added to this are the complaints of the country folk, who after a long time abuse my ears by their right. There presses too the necessity of letting out my farms, most troublesome: so rare is it to find suitable tenants.
30.4. For which reasons I study on sufferance, yet I study. For I both write something and read; but when I read, I feel by comparison how badly I write, although you give me good heart,
30.5. you who compare my little books on the vengeance of Helvidius with Demosthenes' speech against . . . Meidias. This I had indeed in my hands when composing them — not that I might rival it, for that would be presumptuous and almost mad, but that I might imitate and follow it, so far as the difference between the greatest and the least talent, or the dissimilarity of the cases, allowed. Farewell.
31.1. Claudius Pollio desires to be loved by you, worthy of this by the very fact that he desires it, and then because he himself loves you; for scarcely anyone makes this demand except one who does the same. He is besides a man upright, honest, quiet, and almost beyond measure — if anyone is beyond measure — modest.
31.2. When we served together in the army, I observed him not merely as a fellow-soldier. He commanded a cavalry regiment a thousand strong; I, ordered by the consular legate to examine the accounts of the cavalry and infantry units, found in some a great and foul greed and an equal negligence, but in him the highest integrity and a scrupulous diligence.
31.3. Afterwards, promoted to the most important procuratorships, he was corrupted by no opportunity and never swerved from his inborn love of abstinence; he never swelled up in prosperity; he never broke his continuous reputation for humanity by any variety of his offices, and with the same firmness of mind sufficed for his labours as he now endures his leisure.
31.4. This indeed he interrupted and laid aside for a little while, with great credit to himself, when he was taken on by our friend Corellius as an assistant in buying and distributing lands under the liberality of the Emperor Nerva. For with what glory is it worthy that, when there was so great a choice of men, he should have specially pleased so great a man!

title: Letters
text:
31.5. How reverently, how faithfully he honours his friends, you may believe from the last judgements of many, among them that of Annius Bassus, a most weighty citizen, whose memory he prolongs and extends by so grateful a proclamation that he has published a book on his life — for he reveres literature too, as he does the other good arts.
31.6. That is a fine thing, and to be approved by its very rarity, since most men remember the dead only to complain.
31.7. This man, most desirous of your friendship — believe me — embrace, lay hold of, even invite, and love him as though you were repaying a favour. For he who began first is to be requited, not obliged, in the office of love. Farewell.
32.1. I am delighted that the arrival of my friend Tiro was pleasant to you; and that, as you write, on the occasion of the proconsul's coming very many were set free, I rejoice exceedingly. For I desire our native country to be increased in all things indeed, but most of all in the number of its citizens: for that is the firmest ornament of towns.
32.2. This too gladdens me — not as an ambitious man, yet still it gladdens me — that you add that you and I were celebrated both with thanks and with praise. For, as Xenophon says, 'praise is the sweetest of all things to hear,' especially if you think you deserve it. Farewell.
33.1. I prophesy — and my prophecy does not deceive me — that your histories will be immortal; and so all the more — I will frankly confess it — I desire to be inserted in them.
33.2. For if it is usually our care that our face should be portrayed by the best artist, ought we not to wish that our deeds should find a writer and herald like yourself?
33.3. I point out, then — though it cannot escape your diligence, since it is in the public records — yet I point it out, that you may the more believe, how pleasant it will be to me if my deed, the credit of which grew through its danger, you should adorn by your genius and your testimony.
33.4. The Senate had assigned me, with Herennius Senecio, as advocate of the province of Baetica against Baebius Massa, and, Massa being condemned, had decreed that his property be kept under public guard. Senecio, having discovered that the consuls would be free for petitions, met me and said: 'With the harmony with which we have carried out the accusation laid upon us, let us approach the consuls and ask that they not allow the dispersal of the property which ought to be in custody.'
33.5. I answered: 'Since we were assigned as advocates by the Senate, consider whether you think our part is finished now that the Senate's cognizance is concluded.' And he: 'You may set yourself whatever limit you wish, you who have no tie with the province save by your own kindness, and that a recent one; I myself was both born there and was quaestor in it.'
33.6. Then I: 'If that is fixed and settled with you, I will follow you, so that, if any ill-will arise from this, it may not be yours alone.'
33.7. We came to the consuls; Senecio said what the case demanded, and I added something. Scarcely had we fallen silent when Massa, complaining that Senecio had filled not the loyalty of an advocate but the bitterness of an enemy, charged him with impiety.
33.8. Horror in all; but I said: 'I fear, most illustrious consuls, that Massa by his silence has charged me with collusion, in that he did not charge me too as a defendant.' This saying was at once taken up, and afterwards much celebrated in talk.
33.9. The deified Nerva indeed — for even as a private man he attended to whatever was rightly done in public — having sent me a most weighty letter, congratulated not me only but the age, to which there had fallen — so he wrote — an example like those of old.

title: Letters
text:
33.10. These things, however they stand, you will make better known, more famous, greater; though I do not require you to exceed the measure of the deed as done. For history ought not to go beyond the truth, and for honourable deeds the truth suffices. Farewell.
1.1. I made my journey comfortably, except that some of my people contracted illness in the most scorching heat.
1.2. Encolpius indeed, my reader — that delight, that pride of mine — coughed up blood from his throat, made raw by the dust. How sad this is for himself, how bitter for me, if he to whom all my charm in study is owed should be made unfit for study! Who then will read my little books so well, will love them so? Whom will my ears so follow?
1.3. But the gods promise happier things. The blood has stopped, the pain has subsided. Besides, he himself is temperate, we are anxious, the doctors diligent. To this add the healthfulness of the air, the seclusion, the quiet, which promise as much of recovery as of leisure. Farewell.
2.1. Others set out for their estates that they may return the richer; I, that I may return the poorer. I had sold my vintage to dealers who bid eagerly. The price invited them, both what it was then and what it seemed likely to be.
2.2. The hope failed. It would have been easy to remit something to all alike, but not altogether fair. To me, however, it seems above all an excellent thing to practise justice abroad as at home, in great matters as in small, in others' affairs as in one's own. For if faults are equal, the praises too are equal.
2.3. So to all indeed — that none might 'go away ungifted' — I conceded an eighth of the price at which each had bought; then to those who had engaged the largest sums in their purchases I made separate provision. For they had both helped me more and made a greater loss themselves.
2.4. Therefore to those who had bought for more than ten thousand I added, to that common and, as it were, public eighth, a tenth of that sum by which they had exceeded ten thousand.
2.5. I fear I have not expressed it clearly: I will show it more plainly by calculation. If, for instance, any had bought for fifteen thousand, these received both an eighth of the fifteen thousand and a tenth of the five thousand.
2.6. Besides, when I reflected that some had repaid a good part of what they owed, some something, some nothing, I judged it by no means right that those whom good faith in payment had not made equal should be made equal by the kindness of my remission.
2.7. So again, to those who had paid I remitted a tenth of what they had paid. By this means it seemed both that thanks were most fitly returned for the past to each according to his desert, and that for the future all were enticed, alike to buy and to pay.
2.8. This policy, or this easiness, cost me much, but it was worth it. For throughout the whole region both the novelty and the form of the remission are praised. And from those very men whom I treated not by one and the same measure, as the saying goes, but distinctly and by degrees, each went away, the better and more honest he was, the more obliged to me, having learned by experience that with me 'in one and the same honour are the coward and the brave.' Farewell.
3.1. The book I last sent you, you signify, pleases you above all of mine. So thinks a certain most learned man too.
3.2. By which I am the more led to think that neither of you is mistaken, because it is not credible that both should be mistaken, and yet because I flatter myself. For I wish each most recent thing to seem the most finished, and so already now I favour, against this book, the speech which I lately gave to the public, and which I shall share with you as soon as I find a careful carrier.

title: Letters
text:
3.3. I have raised your expectation, which I fear the speech, once taken in hand, may disappoint. Meanwhile, all the same, await it as one likely to please — and perhaps it will please. Farewell.
4.1. You do most rightly in preparing to write of the Dacian war. For what material is so recent, so abundant, so lofty, so finally poetic and, though in matters most true, so fabulous?
4.2. You will tell of new rivers led over the land, of new bridges thrown across rivers, of mountain precipices held by camps, of a king driven from his palace, driven even from life, yet despairing of nothing; besides these, of two triumphs celebrated, of which the one was the first over an unconquered nation, the other the last.
4.3. There is one difficulty, but the greatest: that to equal these things in the telling is arduous, immense, even for your genius, although it rises to the loftiest heights and grows with the most splendid works. There is some labour too in this, that barbarous and savage names — above all the king's own — should not jar in Greek verse.
4.4. But there is nothing that may not, by art and care, if it cannot be conquered, at least be softened. Besides, if it is granted to Homer to contract, extend, and inflect soft and Greek words for the smoothness of his verse, why should not a like boldness be granted to you, especially when it is not over-nice but necessary?
4.5. So, having invoked the gods after the right of poets — and among the gods that very one whose deeds, works, and counsels you are about to tell — let out the ropes, spread the sails, and, if ever you did, be borne along with your whole genius. For why should not I too be poetic with a poet?
4.6. This I bargain for now: that you send me each first part as soon as you have finished it — nay, even before you finish, just as the parts shall be, fresh and rough and still like things newborn.
4.7. You will reply that pieces cannot please as well taken separately as woven together, nor begun as well as finished. I know. So by me too they shall be valued as begun, regarded as limbs, and shall await your final polish in my desk. Allow me to have this, above the rest, as a pledge of your love, that I may know even those things which you would wish no one to know. Farewell.
5.1. Our friend Macrinus has received a grievous wound: he has lost his wife of singular example, even if she had lived of old. He lived with her thirty-nine years without quarrel, without offence. What reverence she showed her husband, when she herself deserved the greatest! How many and how great virtues, drawn from different ages, she gathered and blended!
5.2. Macrinus has indeed a great solace, that he held so great a good so long; but from this he is the more embittered, that he has lost it; for the grief of being deprived grows with the enjoyment of pleasures.
5.3. So I shall be in suspense for this most dear friend, until he can admit distractions and bear a scar — which nothing brings on so well as necessity itself, and length of days, and a surfeit of grief. Farewell.
6.1. You must already know from my letter that I lately noted the monument of Pallas under this inscription: 'To him the Senate, for his loyalty and devotion towards his patrons, decreed the praetorian insignia and fifteen million sesterces, with the honour of which he was content.'
6.2. Afterwards it seemed to me worth the trouble to seek out the decree of the Senate itself. I found it so copious and effusive that that most arrogant inscription seemed modest and even humble. Let them set themselves beside it and mingle with it — I do not say those men of old, the Africani, the Achaici, the Numantini, but these of recent times, the Marii, the Sullae, the Pompeii — I will not go further: they will lie below the praises of Pallas.

title: Letters
text:
6.3. Shall I think those who decreed these things witty, or wretched? I would say witty, if wit became the Senate; wretched — but no one is so wretched as to be forced to such things. Was it then ambition and a lust for advancement? But who is so mad as to wish to advance, through his own and the state's disgrace, in that commonwealth in which this was the use of the most flourishing rank, that he might be the first in the Senate to praise Pallas?
6.4. I pass over that praetorian insignia are offered to Pallas a slave — for they are offered by slaves; I pass over that they decree he should be not merely exhorted but even compelled to wear gold rings; for it would have been against the majesty of the Senate, if a man of praetorian rank should wear iron ones.
6.5. These are trifling and to be passed by; but this is to be recorded, that in the name of Pallas the Senate — nor was the senate-house ever afterwards expiated — in the name of Pallas the Senate gives thanks to the Emperor, because both he himself had made mention of him with the highest honour, and had given the Senate the opportunity of testifying its goodwill towards him.
6.6. For what could be finer for the Senate than that it should appear sufficiently grateful towards Pallas? It is added: 'That Pallas, to whom all confess themselves obligated each to the utmost of his power, may most deservedly receive the fruit of his singular loyalty and singular industry.' You would believe the empire's frontiers had been extended, armies restored to the republic.
6.7. To these is joined: 'Since to the Senate and people of Rome no more pleasing occasion of liberality could be presented than if they might help the means of the most abstinent and faithful guardian of the imperial wealth.' This then was the Senate's prayer, this the chief joy of the people, this the most welcome occasion of liberality — if it might fall out to help the means of Pallas by a draining of the public wealth.
6.8. Now what follows? That the Senate had wished indeed to decree that fifteen million sesterces should be given from the treasury, and, the further his mind was removed from such desires, the more earnestly to beg of the public father that he should compel him to yield to the Senate.
6.9. This indeed was all that was lacking: that public authority should treat with Pallas, that Pallas should be asked to yield to the Senate, that to that most arrogant abstinence the Emperor himself should be summoned as patron and advocate, lest he should spurn the fifteen million sesterces. He spurned it — the only thing he could do more arrogantly than if he had accepted so great a sum publicly offered.
6.10. Yet the Senate carried this too, like one complaining, with praises, and in these very words: 'But since the best of princes and public father, asked by Pallas, had wished that part of the resolution which pertained to giving him fifteen million sesterces from the treasury to be remitted, the Senate testifies that it had both gladly and deservedly begun to decree this sum among his other honours, for his loyalty and diligence to Pallas, yet that it complies in this matter too with the will of its prince, against whom it thought it right in nothing to resist.'
