6.11. Imagine Pallas, as it were, interposing his veto against a decree of the Senate, and moderating his own honours, and refusing the fifteen million sesterces as too much, when he had accepted the praetorian insignia as though it were less;
6.12. imagine the Emperor obeying the entreaties — or rather the command — of his freedman in the Senate's presence; for the freedman commands the patron whom he asks in the Senate; imagine the Senate testifying everywhere that it had deservedly and gladly begun to decree this sum among the rest of Pallas' honours, and would have persevered, had it not complied with the will of its prince, against whom it was not right to resist in anything. Thus, that Pallas might not carry off the fifteen million sesterces from the treasury, his own modesty needed the compliance of the Senate — a Senate that would in this above all not have complied, had it thought it right in any matter not to comply.

title: Letters
text:
6.13. Do you suppose this is the end? Wait awhile and receive greater things: 'And that, since it is useful that the prince's benignity, most prompt to praise and reward those who deserve, should be illustrated everywhere and most of all in those places where those set in charge of his affairs might be incited to imitation, and that the most approved loyalty and innocence of Pallas might by its example provoke a zeal for so honourable an emulation, the resolutions which the best of princes had recited on the twenty-third of January last in that most ample order, and the decrees of the Senate made concerning these matters, should be engraved in bronze, and that bronze be fixed beside the cuirassed statue of the deified Julius.'
6.14. It seemed too little that the senate-house should be witness of such disgraces: a most frequented place was chosen, in which they might be set forth to be read by those present, to be read by those to come. It was resolved to record in bronze all the honours of that most fastidious chattel, both those he had refused and those — so far as concerns the decreers — he accepted. The praetorian insignia of Pallas were cut and graven on public and eternal monuments, as though they were ancient treaties, as though sacred laws.
6.15. So great was the — I know not what to call it — that the prince, the Senate, Pallas himself wished to be fixed before all men's eyes: Pallas his insolence, the Emperor his patience, the Senate its humility. Nor were they ashamed to set a reason against the baseness — an excellent and fine reason, forsooth: that by the example of Pallas' rewards the rest might be provoked to a zeal of emulation.
6.16. Such was the cheapness of honours — even of those which Pallas did not disdain. Yet there were found men born in honourable station who sought and desired what they saw given to a freedman, promised to slaves.
6.17. How glad I am that I did not fall upon those times, for which I blush as much as if I had lived in them! I do not doubt that you are affected likewise. I know how living and freeborn is your spirit: so it is the easier for you to believe that I, though in certain places I may perhaps have carried my indignation beyond the measure of a letter, have grieved too little rather than too much. Farewell.
7.1. Neither as master to master nor as pupil to pupil — for so you write — but as master to pupil — for you are the master, I the contrary; and indeed you call me back to school, while I still prolong the Saturnalia — you have sent me a book.
7.2. Could I have made a longer hyperbaton, and by this very thing prove that I am one who ought to be called not only not your master but not even your pupil? Yet I will take on the master's part and exert over your book the right you have given, the more freely because I shall send you nothing of mine meanwhile in which you may take your revenge. Farewell.
8.1. Have you ever seen the spring of Clitumnus? If not yet — and I think not yet, otherwise you would have told me — see it; which I — I regret my slowness — lately saw.
8.2. A modest hill rises, wooded and shady with ancient cypress. Beneath it the spring comes out and is forced up through many veins, but unequal ones, and, having struggled free, opens out into the pool it makes, with a broad bosom, clear and glassy, so that you can count the coins thrown in and the gleaming pebbles.
8.3. Thence it is driven on, not by the slope of the place but by its own abundance and, as it were, weight, a spring still and already a most full river, and even capable of bearing ships; which, meeting it too and striving against it in opposite directions, it carries across and bears on, so strong that in the direction in which it itself hastens, though over level ground, it is not helped by oars, while against it the same river is overcome with great difficulty by oars and poles.

title: Letters
text:
8.4. Both are pleasant to those who float for jest and sport, to vary, as they bend their course, toil with ease and ease with toil. The banks are clad with much ash, much poplar, which the clear stream counts among its number, as if sunk, in a green reflection. The coldness of the water might vie with snows, nor does its colour yield.
8.5. Hard by is an ancient and venerable temple. Clitumnus himself stands, robed and adorned with the bordered toga; the oracular lots declare a present and even prophetic divinity. Scattered round about are several chapels, and as many gods. Each has his own worship, his own name, some indeed their own springs too. For besides that one, as it were the parent of the rest, there are lesser ones distinguished by their source; but they mingle with the river, which is crossed by a bridge.
8.6. This is the boundary of the sacred and the profane: in the upper part it is permitted only to sail, below it even to swim. The people of Hispellum, to whom the deified Augustus gave that place as a gift, provide a bath at public cost, provide lodging too. Nor are there lacking villas which, following the river's charm, stand on its margin.
8.7. In short, there will be nothing from which you will not take pleasure. For you will study too: you will read many things by many men, inscribed on every column and every wall, by which that spring and god are celebrated. Many you will praise, some you will laugh at — though you, indeed, with your humanity, will laugh at none. Farewell.
9.1. It is long since I have taken book or pen in hand; long since I know not what leisure or rest is, or that idle yet pleasant doing of nothing and being nothing: so many affairs of my friends suffer me neither to retire nor to study.
9.2. For no studies are worth so much that the office of friendship should be deserted, which the studies themselves teach is to be guarded most religiously. Farewell.
10.1. The more you desire to see great-grandchildren from us, the sadder will you hear that your granddaughter has miscarried, since, girl-like, she did not know she was pregnant, and on this account omitted some things to be observed by pregnant women, and did things to be omitted. This error she expiated by great proofs, brought into the utmost danger.
10.2. So, as you must take it grievously that your old age is robbed, as it were, of posterity already prepared, so you ought to give thanks to the gods that, while they denied you great-grandchildren for the present, they preserved your granddaughter, and will give back those whom this very fruitfulness, though tried with too little success, makes us hope for the more surely.
10.3. With these same arguments I now exhort, admonish, and strengthen you with which I do myself. For you do not desire great-grandchildren more ardently than I children, to whom I seem about to leave, from my side and yours, an easy path to honours, names widely known, and ancestral images not of yesterday. Only let them be born, and turn this grief of ours into joy. Farewell.
11.1. When I consider your affection towards your brother's daughter, softer even than a mother's indulgence, I understand that what is last is to be announced to you first, so that joy taken in advance may leave no room for anxiety. Though I fear that even after my congratulation you may return to fear, and so rejoice that she is freed from danger as at the same time to shudder that she was in danger.
11.2. Now cheerful, now restored to herself, now to me, she begins to recover, and to measure the crisis past by her convalescing. She was otherwise in the utmost danger — may I be allowed to have said it without harm — through no fault of her own, some fault of her age. Hence the miscarriage, and the sad lesson of a womb unknown.

title: Letters
text:
11.3. So, even if it has not fallen to you to console the loss of your dead brother with a grandson or granddaughter of his, remember nevertheless that this is rather deferred than denied, since she from whom it can be hoped is safe. At the same time excuse to your father this mishap, who finds pardon more readily for women. Farewell.
12.1. This one day I beg off: Titinius Capito is to recite, whom I know not whether I ought rather to hear or to wish to hear. He is an excellent man, and to be numbered among the chief ornaments of the age. He cultivates literature, loves, fosters, advances the studious — the harbour, the bay, the bosom of many who compose anything, the example of all, and, in short, the restorer and reformer of letters themselves, now growing old.
12.2. He lends his house to those who recite, and frequents the reading-halls, not only at his own place, with wonderful kindness; to me at least, if only I was in the city, he never failed. The more disgraceful, then, it would be not to return thanks, the more honourable the cause for returning them.
12.3. Or, if I were worn with lawsuits, should I believe myself bound to one who attended my recognizances; and now, because all my business, all my care is in study, should I be less obligated to one who celebrates me with such diligence, in the one thing wherein I can be obligated — I will not say alone, but certainly most of all?
12.4. But even if I owed him no return, no mutual offices as it were, I should still be moved either by the man's most beautiful genius — and that most gentle, even in the greatest severity — or by the honourableness of his subject. He writes of the deaths of illustrious men, among them of some most dear to me.
12.5. I seem, then, to perform a pious office, and at the funeral eulogies, late indeed but for that reason the truer, of those whose obsequies I was not permitted to celebrate, to be present. Farewell.
13.1. I approve that you have read my little books with your father. It tends to your progress to learn from a most eloquent man what is to be praised, what to be blamed, and at the same time to be so trained that you grow used to telling the truth.
13.2. You see whom you should follow, whose footsteps you ought to fill. O happy you, to whom it has fallen to have one and the same model, the best and the most closely joined, who, in short, have one above all to imitate, to whom nature has willed that you be most like! Farewell.
14.1. Since you are most skilled both in private law and in public, of which the senatorial is a part, I wish to hear from you above all whether I erred lately in the Senate or not — not for the past, for that is too late, but so that for the future, if anything similar should occur, I may be instructed.
14.2. You will say: 'Why do you ask what you ought to have known?' The servitude of former times brought, as upon other excellent arts, so upon the law of the Senate too, a kind of forgetfulness and ignorance.
14.3. For how few are so patient as to be willing to learn what they will not have occasion to use? Add that it is hard to retain what you have received unless you practise it. So liberty restored has caught us untrained and inexpert; fired by its sweetness, we are compelled to do certain things before we know them.
14.4. Now in old times it was the custom that we should learn from our elders not by the ears only but also by the eyes those things which we ourselves were soon to do, and by certain alternations to hand down to our juniors.

title: Letters
text:
14.5. Hence young men were at once steeped in military service, that they might learn to command by obeying, to lead while they followed; hence those about to seek office stood at the doors of the senate-house, and were spectators of the public council before they were partners in it.
14.6. Each had his own father for master, or he who had no father, the greatest and oldest man in his father's place. What power belongs to those who lay matters before the Senate, what right to those who vote, what force to the magistrates, what liberty to the rest, where one must yield, where resist, what the time for silence, what the measure of speaking, how to distinguish conflicting opinions, how to carry out those who add something to earlier ones — in short, all the senatorial custom — they were taught by examples, the surest means of learning.
14.7. But we young men were indeed in the camps; yet at a time when virtue was suspect, sloth in esteem; when commanders had no authority, soldiers no reverence; when there was nowhere command, nowhere obedience, all things loosened, confused, and even turned to their contrary — things, in short, rather to be forgotten than held.
14.8. We likewise looked into the senate-house, but a senate-house trembling and tongue-tied, when to say what you wished was dangerous, what you did not wish, wretched. What could then be learned, what profit was there in having learned, when the Senate was summoned either to the utmost idleness or to the utmost wickedness, and, kept for sport now, now for grief, never decreed serious things, and sad ones often?
14.9. The same evils, now as senators, now as partners in the evils, we saw and endured for many years; by which our talents for the future too were dulled, broken, bruised.
14.10. Short is the time — for every time is the shorter the happier it is — in which it pleases us to know what we are, in which it pleases us to exercise what we know. So with the more right I ask, first, that you pardon my error, if there is any error, and then that you remedy it by your knowledge, which has always made it its care to treat public law as well as private, ancient as well as recent, rare as well as common.
14.11. And I think that even to those whom frequent dealing with very many matters suffered to be ignorant of nothing, the kind of question I bring to you was either not sufficiently familiar or even untried. So I am the more excusable if perchance I have slipped, and you the more worthy of praise, if you can teach even that which is in doubt whether you yourself had learned it.
14.12. A motion was being put concerning the freedmen of the consul Afranius Dexter, slain — it was uncertain whether by his own or his people's hand, by crime or by obedience. These one man — Who? I; but it matters not — judged should be freed from punishment after the inquiry by torture; another, that they should be relegated to an island; another, that they should be punished with death. Of these opinions the difference was so great that they could not but stand singly.
14.13. For what has killing in common with relegating? Truly no more than relegating with acquitting; although the opinion that relegates is somewhat nearer to the one that acquits than to the one that kills — for either of these leaves life, the latter takes it away — while meanwhile both those who would punish with death and those who would relegate sat together, and by a temporary pretence of concord deferred their discord.
14.14. I demanded that to the three opinions their own number should belong, and that two should not join by a brief truce. So I insisted that those who thought they should suffer capital punishment should withdraw from the one who relegated, nor meanwhile band together against the acquitters, though about to disagree presently; because it mattered little whether the same thing displeased those to whom the same thing had not been pleasing.

title: Letters
text:
14.15. This too seemed to me most strange: that he indeed who had voted the freedmen should be relegated, the slaves punished, was compelled to divide his opinion; but that this man who would punish the freedmen with death should be numbered with the one who relegated. For if it was right that one man's opinion should be divided, because it embraced two matters, I could not see how the opinions of two men, voting things so different, could be joined.
14.16. And so allow me, before you as if there, with the matter concluded as if still entire, to render the reasoning of my judgement, and to put together at leisure now what I then said piecemeal, with many interrupting.
14.17. Let us suppose that three judges in all were assigned to this case; that to one of these it had seemed good that the freedmen should perish, to another that they should be relegated, to the third that they should be acquitted. Will the two opinions, with combined forces, destroy the last, or will each separately be worth as much as the other, nor will the first be able to be joined with the second any more than the second with the third?
14.18. Therefore in the Senate too they ought to be counted as contrary which are spoken as different. But if one and the same man should vote both that they perish and that they be relegated, could they, by the opinion of one man, both perish and be relegated? Or, in short, would it be reckoned a single opinion that joined things so different?
14.19. How then, when one votes that they be punished, another that they be relegated, can it seem one opinion that is uttered by two, which would not seem one if uttered by one? What? Does not the law plainly teach that the opinions of him who kills and him who relegates ought to be separated, when it orders the division to be made thus: 'You who vote for this, go to this side; you who vote for everything else, go to that side as you think'? Examine each word and weigh it: 'you who vote for this,' that is, who think they should be relegated, 'to this side,' that is, to that on which he sits who voted that they be relegated.
14.20. From which it is manifest that those who think they should be killed cannot remain on the same side. 'You who vote for everything else': you observe how the law, not content to say 'else,' has added 'everything.' Is there any doubt, then, that those who would kill vote 'everything else' than those who would relegate? 'Go to that side as you think': does not the law itself seem to call, compel, and drive those who dissent to the opposite side? Does not the consul too, where each must remain, whither he must cross, not only by the solemn words but by hand and gesture point out?
14.21. But it will come about, you say, that if the opinions of him who kills and him who relegates are divided, the one that acquits will prevail. What is that to those who vote? Whom it certainly does not become to fight by every art, by every device, lest the milder course prevail. Yet those who punish and those who relegate ought first to be compared with the acquitters, and then with each other. Just as in certain spectacles the lot sets aside and reserves someone to contend with the victor, so in the Senate there are first contests and second; and of two opinions, the one that has come off superior the third awaits.
14.22. What of this, that, the first opinion approved, the rest are destroyed? By what reasoning, then, can there be not one and the same place for opinions, of which none has any after?

title: Letters
text:
14.23. I will repeat it more plainly. Unless, when he who relegates speaks his opinion, those who would punish at once withdraw to another side at the very beginning, they will dissent in vain afterwards from him with whom shortly before they had agreed.
14.24. But why do I act like one teaching? when I wish to learn whether the opinions ought to be divided or to be taken singly. I obtained indeed what I demanded; none the less I ask whether I ought to have demanded it. How did I obtain it? He who thought the extreme penalty should be exacted, conquered — I know not whether by the law, but certainly by the equity of my demand — gave up his own opinion and went over to the one relegating, fearing, of course, lest, if the opinions were divided, as otherwise seemed likely to happen, the one voting acquittal should prevail by number. For there were far more in this one than in the two single ones.
14.25. Then those too who were drawn by his authority, deserted when he crossed over, abandoned the opinion forsaken by its own author, and followed, as though a deserter, the leader they had been following.
14.26. So out of three opinions two were made, and of the two one prevailed, the third being driven out, which, since it could not overcome both, chose by which of the two it should be defeated. Farewell.
15.1. I have burdened you with so many volumes sent at once; but I have burdened you, first, because you required it, then because you wrote that your vintage there was so scanty that I knew well you would have leisure, as the common saying goes, to read a book.
15.2. The same is reported from my little fields. So it will be lawful for me too to write what you may read, if only there be the means of buying paper; or else, of necessity, whatever we have written, good or bad, we shall delete. Farewell.
16.1. The illnesses of my people have worn me down — their deaths too, and those of young men at that. There are two consolations, by no means equal to so great a grief, yet consolations: one, the freedom of manumitting — for I seem not to have lost altogether before their time those whom I lost already free; the other, that I allow my slaves too to make wills, as it were, and observe them as legal.
16.2. They commend and ask what they please; I obey as if bidden. They divide, give, leave, so long as it be within the household; for to slaves the household is a kind of commonwealth and, as it were, a city.
16.3. But though I rest in these consolations, I am weakened and broken by that very humanity which led me to allow this very thing. Yet I should not on that account wish to become harder. Nor am I unaware that others call such mishaps nothing more than a loss, and on that account seem to themselves great men and wise. Whether they are great and wise, I do not know; men they are not.
16.4. For it is a man's part to be moved by grief, to feel, yet to resist and admit consolations — not to have no need of consolations. But of these things perhaps more than I should; yet fewer than I would. For there is a certain pleasure even in grieving, especially if you weep in the bosom of a friend, with whom your tears find either praise prepared or pardon. Farewell.
17.1. Is the sky with you too harsh and stormy? Here are continual tempests and frequent floods. The Tiber has overflowed its bed and pours deeply over its lower banks;
17.2. though drained off by the channel which the most provident Emperor made, it presses on the valleys, swims over the fields, and wherever the ground is level, is seen in place of the ground. Thence the rivers which it usually receives and carries down mixed with itself, it drives back as it were to meet them, and so covers with alien waters the fields it does not itself touch.

title: Letters
text:
17.3. The Anio, most delicate of streams, and therefore, as it were, invited and detained by the villas adjoining it, has for the most part broken and swept away the woods that shade it; it has undermined hills, and, dammed in many places by the mass of what falls, while it seeks its lost path, has driven down houses and flung itself up and over the ruins.
17.4. Those whom that storm caught on higher ground have seen, in one place, the appointments of the rich and their heavy furniture; in another, the implements of the farm; here oxen, ploughs, drivers; there herds loosed and free; and among these, the trunks of trees, or the beams and roofs of villas, floating widely and in disorder.
17.5. Nor were even those places free from the calamity which the river did not reach. For in place of the river there was the ceaseless rain, and the whirlwinds hurled from the clouds; the works by which precious fields are enclosed were thrown down; monuments shaken and even overturned. Many were crippled, overwhelmed, crushed by such disasters, and the losses were increased by mourning.
17.6. Lest anything similar happen with you, I fear in proportion to the danger; and I ask you, if nothing of the kind has occurred, to relieve my anxiety as soon as possible — but even if such a thing has occurred, to announce that too. For it matters little whether you suffer adversity or expect it; except that there is a limit to grieving, none to fearing. For you grieve as much as you know has happened, but fear as much as may happen. Farewell.
18.1. It is surely false, what is commonly believed, that men's wills are the mirror of their characters, since Domitius Tullus appeared far better in death than in life.
18.2. For though he had given himself up to be courted by legacy-hunters, he left his daughter heir — who was common to him and to his brother, because he had adopted her, born of his brother. He honoured his grandchildren with very many and most welcome legacies, honoured even his great-granddaughter. In short, all was full of the utmost devotion, and the more unexpected for that.
18.3. So various were the conversations throughout the city: some called him false, ungrateful, forgetful, and, while they assailed him, betrayed themselves by the most disgraceful confessions, complaining of a father, a grandfather, a great-grandfather as of one childless; others, on the contrary, extolled with praises this very thing, that he had cheated the wicked hopes of men, whom to deceive thus befits the manners of the age. They added too that it was not free to him to die by another will: for he had not left his wealth to his daughter, but given it back, having been enriched through his daughter.
18.4. For Curtilius Mancia, hating his son-in-law Domitius Lucanus — Tullus' brother — had made his daughter, Mancia's granddaughter, his heir on this condition, that she be released from her father's hand. The father released her, the uncle adopted her, and so, the will being circumvented, the brother and partner recalled the emancipated daughter into his brother's power by the fraud of adoption, and that with the most ample wealth.
18.5. It was otherwise, as it were, given to those brothers by fate that they should grow rich against the will of those by whom they were made so. Indeed Domitius Afer, who took them into his name, left a will declared eighteen years before, and afterwards so disapproved by himself that he had their father's property proscribed.
18.6. Wonderful was that man's harshness, wonderful these men's good fortune: his harshness, who struck from the number of the citizens one whom he had even as partner in his children; these men's good fortune, who succeeded in their father's place to the man who had taken their father away.

title: Letters
text:
18.7. But this inheritance of Afer's too, like the rest gained together with his brother, was to be transmitted to the brother's daughter, by whom Tullus had been made sole heir and preferred to his daughter, that he might be reconciled. So the more praiseworthy is the will, which devotion, loyalty, and modesty wrote, in which, in short, to all the connections by marriage thanks were returned according to each one's office, returned to his wife too.
18.8. She received most charming villas, received much money — an excellent and most patient wife, and the better deserving of her husband the more she was reproached for marrying him. For a woman illustrious in birth, upright in character, declining in years, long a widow, once a mother, seemed to have followed too little becomingly a marriage with a rich old man so undone by disease that he might have been a weariness to a wife whom he had married young and sound.
18.9. For, distorted and broken in all his limbs, he surveyed his great wealth with his eyes alone, nor was he even moved in his bed except by others; indeed — foul and pitiable to tell — he offered his teeth to be washed and rubbed. He was often heard, when he complained of the indignities of his infirmity, to say that he daily licked the fingers of his own slaves.
18.10. Yet he lived and wished to live, sustained chiefly by his wife, who by perseverance had turned the blame of a marriage begun into glory.
18.11. You have all the tales of the city; for Tullus is the whole subject of all tales. The auction is awaited: for he was so wealthy that he furnished his most ample gardens, on the very day he bought them, with very many and most ancient statues; so many most beautiful works he had in his storehouses, which he neglected. In your turn, if anything there is worthy of a letter, do not grudge it.
18.12. For while men's ears are gladdened by novelty, we are instructed for the conduct of life by examples. Farewell.
19.1. Both my joy and my solace are in literature, and there is nothing so glad that these do not make it gladder, nothing so sad that it is not less sad through these. So, troubled by my wife's illness and the danger of my people, and indeed by the death of some, I fled to study as the one relief of grief, which makes me understand adversity more keenly but bear it more patiently.
19.2. It is my custom, with whatever I am about to put into men's hands, first to examine it by the judgement of my friends, above all by yours. So if ever, now give attention to the book which you will receive with this letter, because I fear that I, being sad, gave too little attention myself. For I could command grief that I should write, but not that I should write with a mind free and glad. Moreover, as joy comes from study, so studies come from cheerfulness. Farewell.
20.1. To learn the things for which we are used to set out on a journey and to cross the sea, we neglect when they are set before our eyes — whether because it is so ordered by nature that, careless of what is near, we pursue what is far off; or because all desire for things grows faint when the opportunity is easy; or because we put it off as though we should often see what it is given us to see whenever we wish to behold it.
20.2. For whatever cause, there are very many things in our city and near the city which we know not by our eyes only but not even by our ears, which, had Achaia, Egypt, Asia, or any other land fruitful in marvels and ready to commend them produced them, we should have heard, read, and surveyed.

title: Letters
text:
20.3. I myself, at least, lately heard and saw at once what I had neither heard nor seen before. My wife's grandfather had required me to inspect his estates at Ameria. As I walked through them, there was shown me, lying below, a lake named Vadimon; and certain incredible things were told of it.
20.4. I came to it. The lake is shaped like a wheel lying flat, and equal on every side: no bay, no obliquity; all measured and even, and, as it were, hollowed and cut out by an artist's hand. The colour is whiter than azure, greener and deeper; there is a smell of sulphur and a medicinal taste; a power by which broken bones are made whole. Its extent is moderate, yet such as to feel the winds and to swell with waves.
20.5. No ship is on it — for it is sacred — but islands float upon it, all grassy with reed and rush, and whatever else a more fertile marsh and that very edge of the lake puts forth. Each has its own shape and size; the margin of all is rubbed smooth, because, often dashed against the shore or against one another, they wear and are worn. The height of all is equal, equal their lightness; for in the likeness of a keel they go down with a shallow base.
20.6. This is seen on every side, the same mass alike poised above the water and sunk in it. Sometimes joined and coupled they are like solid land; sometimes, the winds being at variance, they are dispersed; sometimes, left to themselves by the calm, they float singly.
20.7. Often the smaller cling to the greater, like little boats to merchant-ships; often the greater and smaller alike, as it were, undertake a course and a contest; then again, all driven to the same place, they push the land forward where they have stood, and now here, now there, give back and take away the lake, and only then, when they have held the middle, do they not contract it.
20.8. It is known that cattle, following the grass, are wont to advance onto those islands as onto the farthest bank, nor to perceive the moving ground until, snatched from the shore as if carried out and set there, they are frightened by the lake surrounding them on every side; then, going off whither the wind has borne them, they feel no more that they have descended than they had felt that they had ascended.
20.9. The same lake is poured out into a river, which, when it has shown itself a little to the eyes, is sunk in a cavern and flows deeply hidden; and, if it receives anything before it is drawn down, keeps and brings it forth.
20.10. These things I have written to you, because I believed them no less unknown to you than to me, and no less welcome. For natural works delight you as they do me, nothing equally. Farewell.
21.1. As in life so in study, I think it most beautiful and most humane to blend severity with courtesy, lest the one pass into gloom, the other into wantonness.
21.2. Led by this reasoning, I vary my graver works with light pieces and jests. To bring these forward I chose a most fitting time and place, and, that they might even now grow used to be heard both by men at leisure and in the dining-room, in the month of July, when lawsuits are most at rest, having set chairs before the couches, I placed my friends.
21.3. It chanced that on the same morning I was asked to a sudden advocacy, which gave me cause to speak a preface. For I begged that no one should reproach me as irreverent towards my work, because, being about to recite — though to friends and a few, that is, again to friends — I had not abstained from the forum and from business. I added that I follow this order in writing too, that I prefer necessities to pleasures, serious things to agreeable, and write first for my friends, then for myself.

title: Letters
text:
21.4. The book was both various in little works and in metres. So we are wont, who trust our talent too little, to flee the danger of satiety. I recited for two days. This the approval of the hearers required; and yet, while others pass over certain things and reckon it to their credit that they pass them over, so I omit nothing, and even say that I do not omit anything. For I read everything that I may correct everything, which cannot happen to those who recite selected passages.
21.5. That, you say, is more modest and perhaps more reverent; but this is more open and more loving. For he loves who thinks himself so loved that he does not dread giving weariness; and, besides, what do companions afford, if they come together for their own pleasure's sake? He is fastidious and like a stranger who would rather hear a friend's book good than make it so.
21.6. I do not doubt that you, with your other affection for me, desire to read as soon as possible this book still new from the press. You shall read it, but revised — which was the cause of reciting it; and yet some parts of it you already know. These, corrected afterwards or — as sometimes happens with longer delay — made worse, you will recognize as if new and rewritten. For when very many things are changed, those too seem changed which remain. Farewell.
22.1. Do you know those men who, slaves to all lusts, are angry at others' vices as though they envied them, and most severely punish those whom they most imitate? — whereas nothing more becomes even those who need no one's clemency than gentleness.
22.2. And for my part I think that man best and most faultless who so forgives others as if he himself sinned daily, and so abstains from sin as if he forgave no one.
22.3. So this let us hold at home, this abroad, this in every kind of life: that we be implacable to ourselves, but easy to be entreated even by those who know not how to grant pardon save to themselves; and let us commit to memory what that gentlest and therefore greatest man Thrasea was often wont to say: 'He who hates vices, hates men.' You ask perhaps what has moved me to write this.
22.4. Lately a certain man — but better face to face; though not even then. For I fear lest, while I disapprove, to pursue, carp at, and report it should be at odds with that very thing I am at this moment teaching. Whoever he be, of whatever sort, let him be passed over in silence, whom to mark out matters nothing to the example, not to mark out matters much to humanity. Farewell.
23.1. Grief has taken from me, shaken off, snatched away all my studies, all my cares, all my distractions — grief most grievous, which I have conceived from the death of Junius Avitus.
23.2. He had assumed the broad stripe in my house, had been helped by my support in seeking offices; besides, he so loved me, so reverenced me, that he used me as the moulder of his character, as it were his master.
23.3. Rare is this in our young men. For how few yield as inferior either to another's age or to his authority? At once they are wise, at once they know everything, reverence no one, imitate no one, and are themselves their own examples. But not Avitus, whose chief prudence was this, that he thought others more prudent; whose chief learning, that he wished to learn.
23.4. He always consulted me about something, either concerning studies or the duties of life; he always withdrew the better for it; and he had become better either by what he had heard, or simply by what he had asked.

title: Letters
text:
23.5. What obedience he showed to Servianus, a most exact man! whom, as legate, he so understood and won as tribune that, when he passed from Germany into Pannonia, he followed him not as a fellow-soldier but as a companion and attendant. With what industry, what modesty, as quaestor he was no less pleasant and welcome to his consuls — and he had several — than useful! With what running to and fro, what vigilance he sought this very aedileship, of which he was snatched before his time! Which above all exasperates my grief.
23.6. There hover before my eyes his vain labours, his fruitless prayers, and the honour which he only deserved; there returns to my mind that broad stripe assumed among my household gods, there return those my first and those my last votes for him, those talks, those consultations.
23.7. I am moved by his very youth, moved by the misfortune of his kinsfolk. He had a parent advanced in years, he had a wife whom a year before he had taken as a maiden, he had a daughter whom a little before he had acknowledged. So many hopes, so many joys one day turned to their opposite.
23.8. Lately designated aedile, a new husband, a new father, he left his office untouched, his mother bereaved, his wife widowed, his daughter an orphan, ignorant of her father. To my tears is added that, absent and ignorant of the impending evil, I learned at once that he was ill and at once that he was dead, lest I should grow used to so grievous a grief through fear. In such torments was I when I wrote this — so that this is all I wrote; for now I can neither think nor speak of anything else. Farewell.
24.1. My love for you compels me, not indeed to instruct — for you need no instructor — yet to admonish you to hold and observe what you know, or else it were better not to know it.
24.2. Consider that you have been sent to the province of Achaia, that true and pure Greece, in which civilization, letters, and even agriculture are believed first to have been discovered; sent to set in order the condition of free cities, that is, to men most fully men, to free men most fully free, who have kept by virtue, by merit, by friendship, in short by treaty and by religion, the right given them by nature.
24.3. Reverence the gods who founded them and the names of the gods; reverence their ancient glory and this very old age, which in a man is venerable, in cities sacred. Let there be with you honour for antiquity, for mighty deeds, for legends too. Take nothing from anyone's dignity, nothing from his liberty, nothing even from his vaunting.
24.4. Have before your eyes that this is the land which sent us our laws, which gave laws not to the conquered but to those who asked, that it is Athens you approach, Lacedaemon you govern; from whom to snatch the remaining shadow and surviving name of liberty is hard, cruel, barbarous.
24.5. You see how, though in sickness slave and free differ in nothing, doctors nevertheless treat the free more gently and kindly. Recall what each city once was, not so as to despise it for having ceased to be; let pride and harshness be far off.
24.6. Nor fear contempt. Is he despised who has command, who has the rods, unless he is base and sordid, and one who first despises himself? Ill does power test its strength by injuries to others, ill is reverence won by terror, and love is far more potent than fear for obtaining what you wish. For fear departs if you withdraw; love remains, and as the one turns into hatred, so the other into reverence.

title: Letters
text:
24.7. You, indeed, again and again — for I will repeat it — ought to remember the very title of your office, and to interpret to yourself how great and of what kind it is to set in order the condition of free cities. For what is more civil than ordering, what more precious than liberty?
24.8. And then, how shameful, if ordering be changed into overthrow, liberty into servitude! Add that you have a contest with yourself: the fame of your quaestorship weighs upon you, which you brought back excellent from Bithynia; the testimony of the Emperor weighs upon you; your tribunate, praetorship, and this very legation given as it were a reward, weigh upon you.
24.9. So the more must you strive that you may not seem to have been more humane, better, more skilled in a far-off province than in one near the city, among subjects than among the free, sent by lot than by judgement, raw and unknown than tried and approved; since it is, besides — as you have often heard, often read — far more disgraceful to lose praise than not to attain it.
24.10. This I would have you believe, what I said at the beginning, that I have written admonishing, not instructing — though instructing too. For I do not fear lest in love I should have exceeded the measure. For there is no danger lest that be too much which ought to be the greatest. Farewell.
1.1. I have often advised you to publish as soon as possible the books which you composed either for yourself or against Planta — or rather both for yourself and against him, for so the subject required; and now especially, having heard of his death, I both urge and advise it.
1.2. For although you have read them to many and given them to many to read, I would not have anyone suppose that they were only begun after his death, which you finished while he was still alive. Let your reputation for steadfastness be preserved. And it will be, if it is known both to the fair-minded and the unfair that the confidence to write was not born to you after your enemy's death, but that the edition, already prepared, was forestalled by his death.
1.3. At the same time you will avoid that saying, 'It is not holy to triumph over the slain.' For what is written of a living man, recited of a living man, is published against the dead too as if still living, if it is published at once. So, if you have anything else in hand, lay it aside for the moment; finish this, which to us who have read it seems long since complete. But let it now seem so to you too, whose delay neither the matter itself requires, and the reckoning of the time cuts short. Farewell.
2.1. You act agreeably in demanding from me not only very many letters but very long ones; in which I have been more sparing, partly because I feared your engagements, partly because I myself was much distracted, for the most part by trifling business, which both calls the mind away and breaks it up. Besides, no further material for writing was given.
2.2. For our condition is not the same as Marcus Tullius', to whose example you summon us. For he had both a most copious genius, and, to match his genius, a variety and a greatness of affairs supplied most abundantly;
2.3. but within what narrow bounds I am confined, even though I be silent you perceive — unless perhaps we wish to send you scholastic and, so to speak, shadowy letters.
2.4. But we think nothing less fitting, when we consider your arms, your camp, in short your bugles and trumpets, the sweat, the dust, the suns.
2.5. You have, I think, a fair excuse, which yet I doubt whether I wish to be accepted by you. For it is the mark of the highest love to deny pardon to friends' brief letters, even though you know that there is good reason for them. Farewell.

title: Letters
text:
3.1. One man thinks one thing: I count him most blessed who enjoys the foretaste of a good and lasting reputation, and, sure of posterity, lives with future glory. And to me, had I not the prize of eternity before my eyes, that rich and deep repose would be pleasing.
3.2. For I think all men ought to consider either their immortality or their mortality, and that the former should strive and exert themselves, the latter rest and relax, nor weary their short life with perishable labours, as I see many do, who by a wretched and at the same time thankless show of industry come to despise themselves.
3.3. These things I say to you which I say daily to myself, that I may cease to say them to myself, if you dissent; though you will not dissent, you who always meditate something bright and immortal. Farewell.
4.1. I should fear you might think the speech which you will receive with this letter immoderately long, were it not of such a kind that it seems often to begin and often to end. For single charges are contained, as it were, in single cases.
4.2. So you will be able, wherever you begin and wherever you leave off, to read what follows next both as beginnings and as connected wholes, and to judge me longest in the whole, shortest in the parts. Farewell.
5.1. You do excellently — for I inquire — and persevere, in that you commend your justice to the provincials with much humanity; the chief part of which is to embrace each most honourable man, and so to be loved by the lesser as at the same time to be valued by the leading men.
5.2. But most men, while they fear lest they seem to grant too much to the favour of the powerful, win a reputation for awkwardness and even ill-will.
5.3. From which fault you have withdrawn far, I know; but I cannot restrain myself from praising, like one who admonishes, that you keep such measure as to preserve the distinctions of ranks and dignities; which, if they are confounded, disordered, mingled, nothing is more unequal than that very equality. Farewell.
6.1. All this time I have passed in most pleasant quiet among my tablets and little books. 'How,' you say, 'could you in the city?' There were the Circensian games, by which kind of spectacle I am not held in the least. There is nothing new, nothing varied, nothing that it does not suffice to have seen once.
6.2. So I wonder all the more that so many thousands of men should so childishly desire again and again to see horses running, men standing in chariots. If at least they were drawn by the speed of the horses or the skill of the men, there would be some reason; but as it is they favour a rag, they love a rag, and if in the very midst of the course and contest this colour were transferred there, that one here, the zeal and favour would pass with it, and on a sudden they would forsake those drivers, those horses which they recognize from afar, whose names they shout.
6.3. So great is the favour, so great the authority in one most worthless tunic — I say nothing of the common crowd, which is cheaper than a tunic, but with certain serious men too; whom, when I recall them sitting so insatiably over a thing empty, cold, and incessant, I take a certain pleasure that I am not taken by this pleasure.
6.4. And through these days I most gladly bestow my leisure on letters, which others waste in most idle occupations. Farewell.
7.1. You write that you are building. Good; I have found a defence, for now I build with reason, since it is with you. For this too is not unlike, that you build by the sea, I by Lake Como.

title: Letters
text:
7.2. On its shore I have several villas, but two especially, which delight me as much as they busy me.
7.3. The one, set upon the rocks in the manner of Baiae, looks out over the lake; the other, equally in the manner of Baiae, touches the lake. So I am wont to call the former 'tragedy,' the latter 'comedy,' the one because it is raised as if on buskins, the other because it is borne as if on the low socks of comedy. Each has its own charm, and to its possessor is, by that very difference, the more pleasant.
7.4. The latter uses the lake more closely, the former more widely; the latter embraces one bay with a gentle curve, the former divides two from a most lofty ridge; there a straight drive extends along the shore in a long line, here it bends gently along a most spacious terrace; the latter does not feel the waves, the former breaks them; from the latter you can look down on those fishing, from the former you can fish yourself, and cast a hook from your bedroom and almost from your bed, as from a little boat. These are my reasons for adding to each what they lack, on account of what they have in plenty.
7.5. But why should I render you a reason? — with whom for reason it will be enough to do the same. Farewell.
8.1. If, praised by you, I should begin to praise you, I fear I may seem not so much to give my own judgement as to return a favour. But though I may seem so, I think all your writings most beautiful, but most of all those about us.
8.2. This happens for one and the same reason. For both you write best of friends, and I read as best the things written of me. Farewell.
9.1. I most particularly approve that you are so sorrowfully affected by the death of Pompeius Quintianus that you prolong love of the lost by longing — not like most, who love only the living, or rather pretend to love them, and do not pretend even that except towards those whom they see flourishing; for they forget the wretched no otherwise than the dead. But in you is perennial faith and such steadfastness in love that it cannot be ended save by your own death.
9.2. And indeed Quintianus was such a man as it becomes one to love by his own example. He loved the fortunate, protected the wretched, longed for the lost. How great, too, that honesty in his face, what hesitation in his speech, with what even balance gravity and courtesy! What devotion to letters, what judgement! With what piety he lived with a most unlike father! how it did not hinder him from seeming a most excellent man that he was a most excellent son!
9.3. But why do I exasperate your grief? Yet you so loved the young man that you would rather have this than silence about him, especially from me, by whose proclamation you think his life adorned, his memory prolonged, and even that very age in which he was snatched away can be restored. Farewell.
10.1. I desire to obey your precepts; but there is such a dearth of boars that Minerva and Diana, whom you say must be cultivated alike, cannot agree.
10.2. So Minerva only must be served, yet delicately, as befits retirement and summer. On the road, indeed, I extended some lighter pieces, to be deleted at once, with that garrulity by which conversations are strung together in a carriage. To these I added some at the villa, when nothing else was pleasing. So my poems rest, which you think are most conveniently finished among groves and woods.
10.3. I have revised one or two little speeches; though that kind of work is unlovable and unlovely, and more like the labours of the country than its pleasures. Farewell.

title: Letters
text:
11.1. I received your most pleasant letter, especially because you wished that something should be written to you which could be inserted in my books. Material will turn up, either this very thing you point out or another better. For in this there are some stumbling-blocks: look around and they will meet you.
11.2. I did not think there were booksellers at Lugdunum, and so all the more gladly I learned from your letter that my little books are sold there; whose having kept abroad the favour they had won in the city delights me. For I begin to think a thing fairly finished about which, with so great a difference of regions, the judgements of men agree. Farewell.
12.1. A certain man was chastising his son because he bought horses and dogs a little too lavishly. To him, when the young man had withdrawn, I said: 'Look you, did you never do anything for which your father could rebuke you? "Did you," I say. Do you not sometimes do what your son, if he were suddenly the father and you the son, might reprove with equal gravity? Are not all men led by some error? Does not this man indulge himself in this, another in that?'
12.2. This I have written to you, warned by an example of excessive severity, out of our mutual love, lest you too should ever treat your son too harshly and hardly. Consider both that he is a boy and that you have been one, and so use this that you are a father as to remember both that you are a man and the father of a man. Farewell.
13.1. The more zealously and attentively you have read the books I composed on the vengeance of Helvidius, the more earnestly you demand that I write out for you whatever was outside the books and around the books — in short, the whole sequence of the affair, in which through your age you took no part.
13.2. When Domitian was slain, I considered and deliberated with myself that there was a great and beautiful subject for assailing the guilty, avenging the wretched, and putting myself forward. Now among the many crimes of many, none seemed more atrocious than that in the Senate a senator had laid hands on a senator, a man of praetorian rank on a man of consular rank, a judge on a defendant.
13.3. There had been, besides, between Helvidius and me a friendship as great as could be with one who, through fear of the times, hid his great name and equal virtues in retirement; there had been with Arria and Fannia, of whom the one was Helvidius' stepmother, the other the mother of his stepmother. But it was not so much private ties as public right, the indignity of the deed, and the consideration of the example that spurred me.
13.4. And in the first days of restored liberty each man for himself had demanded his enemies — at least the lesser ones — with an unformed and turbid clamour, and at the same time crushed them. I, thinking it both more modest and more steadfast to press a most monstrous defendant not by the common odium of the times but by his own crime, when now that first onset had spent its roar and anger, growing daily fainter, had returned to justice — although then most of all sad, having lately lost my wife — sent to Anteia (she had been married to Helvidius); I asked her to come, because my grief, still fresh, kept me within my threshold.
13.5. When she came, I said: 'It is determined by me not to leave your husband unavenged. Announce it to Arria and Fannia' — they had returned from exile — 'consult yourself, consult them, whether you wish to be enrolled in a deed in which I need no companion; but I would not so favour my own glory as to grudge you a share in it.' Anteia carried the message, nor did they delay.

title: Letters
text:
13.6. Conveniently the Senate was to meet within three days. I always referred everything to Corellius, whom I had found the most provident and wisest of our age: in this, however, I was content with my own counsel, fearing lest he should forbid it; for he was rather hesitant and cautious. But I could not bring myself not to indicate to him on that same day that I would do what I was not deliberating whether to do, having learned by experience that about what you have determined those are not to be consulted whose counsel, once given, you must obey.
13.7. I come into the Senate, I ask leave to speak, I speak for a while with the greatest approval. When I began to touch the charge, to mark out the defendant, though still without a name, on all sides there was outcry against me. One said: 'Let us know who it is about whom you bring an extraordinary motion'; another: 'Who is a defendant before the motion?'; another: 'Let us be safe, we who survive.'
13.8. I listened unperturbed, undismayed: so much avails the honourableness of a thing undertaken, and so much, for confidence or fear, does it matter whether men are unwilling that you should do what you do, or do not approve of it. It would be long to recount all that was hurled from this side and that.
13.9. At last the consul: 'Secundus, you shall speak in your turn, if you wish anything.' 'You had granted,' I said, 'what hitherto you have granted to all.'
13.10. I sit down; other matters are dealt with. Meanwhile a certain one of my consular friends, in a secret and studied speech, takes me to task as having advanced too boldly and incautiously, calls me back, advises me to desist, adds even: 'You have made yourself a marked man to future princes.' 'Be it so,' I said, 'so long as to bad ones.'
13.11. Scarcely had he withdrawn when another: 'What do you dare? Whither do you rush? To what dangers do you expose yourself? Why do you trust in the present, uncertain of the future? You provoke a man already prefect of the treasury and soon to be consul, and besides upheld by what favour, what friendships!' He names a certain man who at that time held a most ample army in the East, not without great and doubtful rumours.
13.12. To this I: 'I have foreseen everything and gone over it before in my mind, nor do I refuse, if so chance should bring it, to pay the penalty for a most honourable deed, while I avenge a most disgraceful one.'
13.13. Now came the time of voting. Domitius Apollinaris, consul designate, speaks; Fabricius Veiento speaks, Fabius Postuminus, Bittius Proculus, colleague of Publicius Certus — about whom the matter was — and stepfather of my wife whom I had lost; after these Ammius Flaccus. All defend Certus, not yet named by me, as if named, and take up the charge as though left, as it were, in the middle, by their defence.
13.14. What else they said it is not necessary to relate: you have it in the books; for I have followed the whole in their own words.
13.15. Against them speak Avidius Quietus and Cornutus Tertullus: Quietus, that it is most unjust that the complaints of the grieving be shut out, and therefore the right of complaint not to be taken from Arria and Fannia, nor does it matter of what rank a man is, but what cause he has;
13.16. Cornutus, that he had been given by the consuls as guardian to Helvidius' daughter at the request of her mother and stepfather; that now too he could not endure to desert the parts of his office, in which, however, he both set a measure to his own grief and bore the most modest feeling of those excellent women; who were content to remind the Senate of Publicius Certus' bloody flattery, and to ask that, if the punishment of a most manifest outrage were remitted, at least a mark be branded on him as if of the censor.

title: Letters
text:
13.17. Then Satrius Rufus, in a middle and ambiguous speech: 'I think,' he said, 'an injury is done to Publicius Certus, if he is not acquitted; he has been named by the friends of Arria and Fannia, named by his own friends. Nor ought we to be anxious; for the same men, we who think well of the man, are also to judge him. If he is innocent, as I both hope and prefer and, until something is proved, believe, you will be able to acquit him.'
13.18. These things they said in the order in which each was called. They come to me. I rise, use the beginning that is in the book, reply to each. It is wonderful with what attention, with what shouts they received everything, who a moment before were crying out against me: so great a change followed either the dignity of the business, or the success of the speech, or the steadfastness of the speaker.
13.19. I finish. Veiento begins to reply; no one allows it; he is shouted down, drowned out, so much so indeed that he said: 'I beg, conscript fathers, that you do not compel me to implore the aid of the tribunes.' And at once Murena the tribune: 'I permit you, most illustrious Veiento, to speak.' Then too there is outcry.
13.20. Amid the delays the consul, the names being called and the division held, dismisses the Senate, and left Veiento almost still standing and trying to speak. He complained much of this — so he called it — insult, in a Homeric verse: 'Old man, in truth the young warriors press you sore.'
13.21. There was hardly anyone in the Senate who did not embrace me, kiss me, and vie in heaping me with praise, because I had restored to public use a custom long since interrupted of taking counsel for the commonwealth by undertaking private enmities; because, in short, I had freed the Senate from the odium with which it was burning among the other orders, in that, severe against the rest, it spared senators alone by a kind of mutual connivance.
13.22. These things were done in the absence of Certus; for he was either, suspecting some such thing, or, as was alleged in excuse, ill. And the Emperor indeed did not refer the motion concerning him to the Senate; yet I obtained what I had aimed at:
13.23. for Certus' colleague received the consulship, Certus a successor, and it came plainly to pass which I had said at the end: 'Let him give back, under the best of princes, the reward which he received from the worst.' Afterwards I gathered together my speech as best I could, and added much.
13.24. It happened by chance — yet not as though by chance — that, the books being published, Certus within a very few days fell ill and died.
13.25. I heard from those who told it that this image flitted before his mind and eyes, as though he saw me threatening him with a sword. Whether this is true I dare not affirm; yet it concerns the example that it should seem true.
13.26. You have a letter which, if you consider the measure of a letter, is no smaller than the books you have read; but you will charge it to yourself, who were not content with the books. Farewell.
14.1. You neither applaud yourself, and I write nothing more in good faith than about you. Whether posterity will have any care for us, I do not know; we at least deserve that it should have some — I do not say by genius, for that is arrogant, but by zeal and labour and reverence for posterity. Let us only go on in the way begun, which, as it has brought few into the light and to fame, so it has brought many out of darkness and silence. Farewell.
15.1. I had fled to my Tuscan estate, that I might do everything at my own pleasure. But this not even in Tuscany: so much am I disquieted by the petitions of the country folk, so many on every side and so querulous, which I read somewhat more unwillingly than my own; for even my own I read unwillingly.

title: Letters
text:
15.2. For I am revising certain little speeches, which after an interval of time is both cold and bitter. My accounts are neglected as though I were absent.
15.3. Sometimes, however, I mount a horse and play the head of the household so far as to ride through some part of my estates, but only by way of exercise. Do you keep up your custom, and to me, thus a countryman, write out the doings of the city. Farewell.
16.1. That you have taken the greatest pleasure from that most abundant kind of hunting I do not wonder, since you write, in the manner of historians, that the number could not be reckoned. For us there is neither leisure nor inclination to hunt: no leisure, because the vintage is in hand; no inclination, because it is scanty.
16.2. Yet we bring down, in place of new must, new little verses, and will send them to you, who most pleasantly demand them, as soon as they shall seem to have fermented. Farewell.
17.1. I have received your letter in which you complain that a most sumptuous dinner was a weariness to you, because buffoons, dancers, and fools wandered among the tables.
17.2. Will you relax something of your frowns? For my part I have nothing of the kind, yet I tolerate those who do. Why then do I not have them? Because nothing of that sort delights me as unexpected or droll, if anything wanton is brought forth by a dancer, anything saucy by a buffoon, anything foolish by a fool.
17.3. I tell you not my reason but my taste. And indeed how many do you suppose there are whom the things by which you and I are taken and led offend, some as silly, some as most tiresome! How many, when a reader or a lyre-player or a comic actor is brought in, call for their shoes, or recline with no less weariness than that with which you endured those — so you call them — monstrosities!
17.4. Let us therefore grant indulgence to others' amusements, that we may obtain it for our own. Farewell.
18.1. With what attention, what zeal, in short what memory you have read my little books, your letter shows. So you yourself make work for yourself, who draw out and invite me to wish to share as many things as possible with you.
18.2. I will do so, yet by parts and as it were in portions, lest I disturb that very memory, to which I give thanks, by continuity and abundance, and, burdened and as it were oppressed, force it to let go single things for many, earlier for later. Farewell.
19.1. You signify that you have read in a certain letter of mine that Verginius Rufus ordered to be inscribed on his tomb: 'Here lies Rufus, who once, Vindex driven back, asserted the empire not for himself but for his country.' You blame him for ordering it, and add too that Frontinus did better and more rightly, in that he forbade altogether that any monument be made for him; and at the end you ask me what I think of each.
19.2. Both I loved; I admired the more him whom you blame, and so admired him that I did not think he could ever be sufficiently praised — whose defence I must now undertake.
19.3. All those who have done some great and memorable thing I judge most worthy not only of pardon but of praise, if they pursue the immortality they have earned, and strive by even their last inscriptions to prolong the fame of a name destined to live.
19.4. Nor do I easily find anyone but Verginius, whose modesty in proclaiming was as great as his glory from the deed.
19.5. I myself am a witness, intimately loved and approved by him, that once only in my hearing he was led so far as to relate this one thing about his affairs: that Cluvius had once said to him thus: 'You know, Verginius, what faith is owed to history; so if you read anything in my histories otherwise than you would wish, I beg you to forgive it.' To which he: 'Do you not know, Cluvius, that I did what I did precisely that it might be free for you to write what you pleased?'

title: Letters
text:
19.6. Come now, let us compare this very Frontinus, in that very point in which he seems to you more reserved and restrained. He forbade a monument to be built, but in what words? 'The expense of a monument is superfluous; the memory of us will endure, if we have deserved it by our life.' Do you think it more reserved to give one's enduring memory to be read throughout the whole world than to mark in one place, in two little verses, what you have done?
19.7. Yet I have no purpose of blaming him, but of defending the other; whose defence before you can be more just than from a comparison with him whom you preferred?
19.8. In my judgement at least neither is to be blamed, both of whom strove towards glory with equal desire by different roads — the one in seeking the titles due to him, the other in preferring to seem to have despised them. Farewell.
20.1. Your letter indeed was the more pleasant to me the longer it was, especially since it spoke throughout of my little books; which that they are a pleasure to you I do not wonder, since you love all that is ours just as you love us.
20.2. I myself am at this very time gathering in a vintage scanty indeed, yet richer than I had expected — if it be gathering in to pluck a grape now and then, to visit the press, to taste the must from the vat, to surprise the town servants, who now preside over the country folk and have left me to my secretaries and readers. Farewell.
21.1. Your freedman, with whom you said you were angry, came to me, and falling at my feet clung to them as if they were yours. He wept much, begged much, was even silent much; in short, he gave me proof of his true repentance. I believe him reformed because he feels he has done wrong.
21.2. You are angry, I know, and angry deservedly, that too I know; but then is the chief praise of mildness, when the cause of anger is most just.
21.3. You loved the man and, I hope, will love him: meanwhile it is enough that you suffer yourself to be entreated. You may be angry again, if he deserve it, and the more excusably, because you were entreated. Allow something to his youth, something to his tears, something to your own indulgence. Do not torment him, do not torment yourself too; for you are tormented when, so gentle, you are angry.
21.4. I fear lest I seem not to ask but to compel, if I join my prayers to his; yet I will join them the more fully and freely, the more sharply and severely I rebuked him, threatening sternly that I would never again ask on his behalf. This to him, whom it behoved to be frightened, not the same to you; for perhaps I shall ask again, and obtain again: only let it be such that it becomes me to ask, you to grant. Farewell.
22.1. The illness of Passennus Paulus has filled me with great anxiety, and that for many most just reasons. He is a most excellent, most honourable man, most devoted to us; besides, in literature he rivals, expresses, reproduces the ancients, Propertius above all, from whom he draws his descent, a true offshoot and so most like him in that wherein Propertius is supreme.
22.2. If you take his elegies in hand, you will read a work polished, soft, pleasant, and plainly written in the house of Propertius. Lately he has turned aside to lyric, in which he so fashions Horace as he does that other in elegy: you would think, if kinship has any force in studies, that he is his kinsman too. Great is his variety, great his versatility: he loves as one most truly, grieves as one most impatiently, praises as one most kindly, jests as one most wittily; in short, he perfects everything as though it were his only work.

title: Letters
text:
22.3. For this friend, for this genius, no less sick in mind than he in body, I have at last recovered him, at last myself. Congratulate me, congratulate too literature itself, which from his danger came to as great a crisis as it will win of glory from his safety. Farewell.
23.1. When I plead, it often befalls me that the Centumviri, after they have long kept themselves within the authority and gravity of judges, suddenly all rise as if conquered and compelled, and praise me;
23.2. often I have brought back from the Senate such fame as I most desired: yet I never took greater pleasure than lately from the conversation of Cornelius Tacitus. He related that at the last Circensian games there had sat beside him a Roman knight. This man, after various learned conversations, had asked: 'Are you Italian or a provincial?' He had answered: 'You know me, and that from my studies.'
23.3. To this the other: 'Are you Tacitus or Pliny?' I cannot express how pleasant it is to me that our names are rendered to literature as belonging to it, not to men; that each of us is known even from his studies to those to whom he is otherwise unknown.
23.4. Something similar happened a very few days before. There was reclining beside me an excellent man, Fadius Rufinus, and above him a fellow-townsman of his own, who that day had come to the city for the first time; to whom Rufinus, pointing me out: 'Do you see this man?' Then much about our studies; and the other: 'It is Pliny,' he said.
23.5. I will confess the truth: I take great fruit of my labour. If Demosthenes was rightly glad that an old woman of Attica recognized him thus, 'This is . . . Demosthenes,' ought I not to rejoice in the celebrity of my name? Indeed I both rejoice and say that I rejoice.
23.6. For I do not fear lest I seem too boastful, when I bring forward about myself the judgement of others, not my own, especially before you, who neither envy anyone's praises and favour ours. Farewell.
24.1. You did well in receiving back into your house and into your heart, at the recall of my letters, a freedman once dear to you. This will gladden you; me at least it gladdens, first because I see you so manageable that in anger you can be governed, then because you attribute so much to me that you either obey my authority or indulge my prayers. So I both praise and give thanks; at the same time I admonish you for the future, that you show yourself placable to the errors of your people, even though there be no one to intercede. Farewell.
25.1. You complain of the throng of camp business, and, as if you enjoyed the deepest leisure, you read, love, and demand our jests and trifles, and not a little incite me to compose the like.
25.2. For I begin from this kind of studies to seek not only delight but glory, after your judgement — a man most learned, most weighty, and above all most truthful in such matters.
25.3. Now the press of affairs distracts me moderately, but still distracts me; when it is finished, I will send something of the same Muses into that most kindly bosom of yours. You will give wings to our little sparrows and doves among your eagles, if at least they please you too; if only themselves, you will see to keeping them shut in cage or nest. Farewell.
26.1. I said of a certain orator of our age, sound indeed and correct, but too little grand and ornate — aptly, as I think: 'He errs in nothing, except that he errs in nothing.'
26.2. For an orator ought to be raised and lifted up, sometimes even to boil over and be carried away, and often to draw near the brink; for usually steeps lie beside lofty and exalted places. The way over the plain is safer but humbler and lower; falls are more frequent for those who run than for those who creep, but for these, if they do not slip, there is no praise, for those, some praise even if they do slip.

title: Letters
text:
26.3. For, as in certain arts, so in eloquence, nothing commends so much as risks. You see those who strive aloft along a rope, what shouts they are wont to raise, when they seem on the very point of falling.
26.4. For those things are most marvellous which are most unexpected, most perilous — and, as the Greeks express it better, hazardous. So the pilot's worth is by no means equal when he sails on a calm and on a troubled sea: then, with none admiring, unpraised, inglorious, he comes into port; but when the ropes whistle, the mast bends, the rudders groan, then is he famous and next to the sea-gods.
26.5. Why do I say this? Because you seemed to me to have noted in my writings certain things as inflated which I thought lofty, as presumptuous which I thought bold, as excessive which I thought full. But it matters very much whether you note things to be blamed or things that stand out.
26.6. For everyone notices what is eminent and prominent; but it must be discerned with keen attention whether it be immoderate or grand, lofty or monstrous. And, to touch Homer above all, what man on either side can fail to mark 'and around great heaven trumpeted' . . . 'and the spear leaned upon the air,' and all that 'nor does so great a wave of the sea roar'?
26.7. But there is need of weighing and balancing, whether these be incredible and empty or magnificent and heavenly. Nor do I now think that I have said, or could say, things like these — I am not so mad — but I wish this to be understood, that the reins of eloquence are to be loosened, and the impulses of genius are not to be checked within the narrowest ring.
26.8. 'But the condition of orators is one, of poets another.' As if indeed Marcus Tullius dared less! Though him I leave aside; for I think there is no doubt. But Demosthenes himself, that standard and rule of the orator, does he restrain and confine himself when he utters those most famous words: 'foul men and flatterers and fiends,' and again, 'I did not wall the city with stones nor with bricks,' and at once, '[did I not think it right] to throw Euboea forward in front of Attica from the sea,' and elsewhere: 'But I think, O men . . . of Athens, by the gods, that he is drunk with the greatness of his deeds'?
26.9. And what is bolder than that most beautiful and longest digression: 'For it is a disease'? What is shorter than these, but in boldness their equal: 'then I, against . . . Python, raging and pouring forth a flood against you'? Of the same stamp: 'but when through greed and wickedness someone, like this man, has grown strong, the first pretext and small stumble has overthrown and dissolved everything.' Like these: 'fenced off from all the rights in the city,' and in the same place: 'you have betrayed pity towards these things, Aristogeiton — nay, you have wholly destroyed it. Do not, then, anchor at the harbours which you yourself have choked and filled with barriers.' And he had said: 'For this man I see no place of these accessible, but all sheer — chasms, gulfs.' And further: 'I fear lest you seem to some to be training one who is forever minded to be wicked among the men of the city.' And not content: 'for I do not suppose that our ancestors built these courts for you, that you might rear up such men in them.' To this: 'but if he is a huckster and a re-huckster and a trafficker of wickedness' — and a thousand such things, to pass over those which Aeschines calls 'marvels,' not 'words.'
26.10. I have fallen into the contrary: you will say that he too is blamed for these things. But see how much greater is he who is reproved than the reprover himself, and the greater for these very things; for in others his force, in these his grandeur shines forth.

title: Letters
text:
26.11. But did Aeschines himself abstain from those things which he carped at in Demosthenes? 'For the orator and the law ought to utter the same thing; but when the law sends forth one voice, the orator another.' In another place: 'then he appears throughout the whole decree.' Again in another: 'but lurking and lying in wait in the hearing, you drive him into illegal speeches.'
26.12. Which he so approved that he repeats it: 'but as in the horse-races, you drive him into the very course of the matter.' And those things more guardedly and compressedly: 'but you make the wound . . . or, seizing him as a pirate sailing through public affairs?'
26.13. I expect that you will stab certain things from this letter — as that 'the rudders groan' and 'next to the sea-gods' — with the same marks as those of which I write; for I understand that, while I sought pardon for the earlier things, I have fallen into those very things which you had noted.
