85.1. Maximus, your freedman and procurator, my lord, I gladly attend with my testimony before you, having found him, throughout all the time we were together, honest, industrious, and diligent, and as most devoted to your interest, so most tenacious of discipline—with that faith which I owe you.
86a.1. Gavius Bassus, my lord, prefect of the Pontic coast, I have found upright, honest, industrious, and amid all this most respectful towards me; and I attend him with my prayer and my vote alike, with that faith which I owe you.
86b.1. . . . than the things he hopes for, equipped by service in your army, to whose discipline he owes it that he is worthy of your indulgence. Before me both soldiers and civilians, by whom his justice and humanity have been thoroughly examined, have borne him testimony in rivalry, both privately and publicly. This I bring to your notice, with that faith which I owe you.
87.1. Nymphidius Lupus, my lord, I had as a fellow-soldier when he was a senior centurion and I myself a tribune, he a prefect: from then I began to love him familiarly. The affection afterwards grew with the very age of our mutual friendship.
87.2. And so I laid hold even of his repose and exacted that he should furnish me with counsel in Bithynia. This he, most affectionately, setting aside the consideration of his ease and old age, both has done and will do.
87.3. For these reasons I count his connections among my own—above all his son, Nymphidius Lupus, an honest, industrious young man, most worthy of his excellent father, and one who will answer to your indulgence, as you may learn from his first trials, since as prefect of a cohort he earned the fullest testimony of those most distinguished men Julius Ferox and Fuscus Salinator. You will crown my joy, my lord, and my congratulation, by the honour of his son.
88.1. I pray, my lord, that you may pass both this birthday and very many others as happily as possible, and that, flourishing in everlasting praise, you may increase the glory of your virtue . . . which, safe and strong, you will augment by works one upon another.
89.1. I acknowledge your prayers, my dear Secundus, in which you beseech that I may pass very many and most happy birthdays while the state of our commonwealth flourishes.
90.1. The people of Sinope, my lord, are short of water; which seems able to be brought, both good and abundant, from the sixteenth milestone. There is, however, right from the source, for a little more than a thousand paces, a suspect and soft stretch of ground, which I have meanwhile ordered to be explored at modest cost, whether it can receive and sustain the work.
90.2. Money will not be wanting, collected by our care, if you, my lord, indulge this kind of work both to the health and to the pleasure of a colony that greatly thirsts.
91.1. As you have begun, my dear Secundus, explore diligently whether that place which you hold suspect can sustain the work of the aqueduct. Nor do I think there ought to be any doubt that water must be brought into the colony of Sinope, if only it can attain it by its own resources, since that matter will contribute very greatly both to the health and to the pleasure of the place.
92.1. The city of the Amiseni, free and confederate, by the benefit of your indulgence uses its own laws. In it a memorial pertaining to a benefit society (eranos) was given to me, which I have appended to this letter, so that you, my lord, may consider what and how far you think ought to be permitted or forbidden.

title: Letters
text:
93.1. The Amiseni, whose memorial you had appended to your letter—if by the laws of those people, which they use by the benefit of their treaty, it is permitted to have a benefit society, we cannot hinder them from having one, the more easily if they use such a contribution not for riots and unlawful assemblies, but for relieving the want of the poorer sort. In other communities, which are bound by our law, a thing of this kind is to be forbidden.
94.1. Suetonius Tranquillus, a most honest, most honourable, most learned man, I have long since, my lord, following both his character and his pursuits, taken into my company, and I have begun to love him the more, the more closely I have now observed him.
94.2. For him two reasons make the right of three children necessary; for he both wins the favourable judgements of his friends and has experienced a marriage of too little good fortune; and what the malignity of fortune has denied him, he must obtain through us from your goodness.
94.3. I know, my lord, how great a benefit I ask, but I ask it of you, whose indulgence I experience in all my desires. For you can gather how greatly I desire it, since I would not ask it in your absence if I desired it but moderately.
95.1. How sparingly I bestow these benefits, my dear Secundus, you at any rate well remember, since even in the Senate I am accustomed to affirm that I have not exceeded the number which I declared before that most august order would suffice me. Yet I have subscribed to your desire, and have ordered it to be entered in my records that I have given the right of three children to Suetonius Tranquillus, on the condition to which I am accustomed.
96.1. It is my custom, my lord, to refer to you all matters about which I am in doubt. For who can better guide my hesitation or instruct my ignorance? I have never been present at trials of Christians; therefore I do not know what is usually punished or inquired into, or to what extent.
96.2. Nor have I hesitated a little whether there is any distinction of ages, or whether those of however tender years differ in nothing from the more robust; whether pardon should be granted to repentance, or whether to one who has been altogether a Christian it should be of no profit to have ceased; whether the name itself, if free from crimes, or the crimes attaching to the name should be punished. Meanwhile, in the case of those who were brought before me as Christians, I have followed this course.
96.3. I asked them themselves whether they were Christians. Those who confessed I asked a second and a third time, threatening punishment; those who persisted I ordered to be led away to execution. For I did not doubt that, whatever it was they confessed, their stubbornness and inflexible obstinacy certainly deserved to be punished.
96.4. There were others of like madness whom, because they were Roman citizens, I marked down to be sent back to the city. Soon, in the very course of handling the matter, as commonly happens, the charge spreading itself, more kinds of cases came up.
96.5. An anonymous memorial was put forward containing the names of many. Those who denied that they were or had been Christians, when, with me leading them, they called upon the gods and made supplication with incense and wine to your image, which I had ordered to be brought for this purpose along with the statues of the deities, and besides reviled Christ—none of which, it is said, those who are truly Christians can be compelled to do—I thought ought to be discharged.

title: Letters
text:
96.6. Others, named by an informer, said that they were Christians and presently denied it; they had been, indeed, but had ceased—some three years before, some more years, not a few even twenty years before. These too all worshipped your image and the statues of the gods, and reviled Christ.
96.7. They affirmed, moreover, that this had been the sum of their fault or error: that they had been accustomed to meet on a fixed day before dawn, and to recite among themselves in turn a hymn to Christ as to a god, and to bind themselves by an oath, not to any crime, but that they would not commit thefts, robberies, or adulteries, that they would not break faith, that they would not deny a deposit when called upon to restore it. When these things were done, it had been their custom to depart and to meet again to take food—but ordinary and harmless food; and this very thing they had ceased to do after my edict, by which, in accordance with your instructions, I had forbidden political clubs to exist.
96.8. I thought it the more necessary to inquire, even by torture, what was the truth, from two maidservants who were called deaconesses. I found nothing other than a depraved and immoderate superstition.
96.9. Therefore, having postponed the cognizance, I hastened to consult you. For the matter seemed to me worthy of consultation, especially on account of the number of those in peril. For many of every age, of every rank, of both sexes also, are being called and will be called into peril. The contagion of this superstition has spread not through the cities only, but through the villages and the countryside as well; yet it seems that it can be checked and corrected.
96.10. At any rate it is sufficiently established that the temples, already nearly deserted, have begun to be frequented, and the solemn rites, long interrupted, to be resumed, and that fodder for the victims is being sold everywhere, for which until now a buyer was very rarely found. From which it is easy to conclude what a multitude of men could be reformed, if there were room for repentance.
97.1. You have followed, my dear Secundus, the course you ought to have followed in examining the cases of those who had been brought before you as Christians. For nothing can be laid down as a general rule, having as it were a fixed form.
97.2. They are not to be sought out; if they are brought before you and convicted, they must be punished, yet in such a way that one who denies that he is a Christian and makes this manifest by the fact itself—that is, by supplicating our gods—though suspected as to the past, may obtain pardon by his repentance. Anonymous memorials put forward ought to have no place in any charge. For it is both of the worst example and unworthy of our age.
98.1. The city of the Amastrians, my lord, both elegant and adorned, has among its chief works a most beautiful and likewise very long street; along the side of which, for its whole length, there stretches what is called a river, but is in truth a most foul sewer, and, as it is foul to the sight with its most unclean appearance, so it is pestilential with its most loathsome smell.
98.2. For which reasons it concerns no less the health than the seemliness of the place that it be covered over; which will be done if you permit, with us taking care that money too be not wanting for a work as great as it is necessary.
99.1. It is reasonable, my dear Secundus, that the water which flows through the city of the Amastrians be covered over, if, uncovered, it harms the public health. That money be not wanting for this work, I am sure you will see to it, according to your diligence.

title: Letters
text:
100.1. The vows pledged the previous year, my lord, we have paid, eager and joyful, and have undertaken new ones again, the devotion of soldiers and provincials vying together, praying the gods that they may keep you and the commonwealth flourishing and safe with that kindness which, beyond your great and very many virtues, you have deserved by your especial holiness, your obedience to the gods, and your honour towards them.
101.1. That you, together with the provincials, with most joyful accord, have paid your vows to the immortal gods for my safety, with me leading, and have pledged them for the future, I have learned with pleasure, my dear Secundus, from your letter.
102.1. The day on which the protection of the human race was transferred to you by a most fortunate succession, we have celebrated with due reverence, commending to the gods, the authors of your rule, both the public vows and the public rejoicings.
103.1. That the day of my accession was celebrated, with due joy and reverence, by the soldiers and provincials, with you leading, I have learned with pleasure from your letter.
104.1. Valerius Paulinus, my lord, has left me, with the exception of Paulinus, the rights over his Latins; of whom I ask that you grant the rights of Roman citizens to three for the present. For I fear it may be excessive to invoke your indulgence for all alike, which I ought to use the more modestly the more fully I experience it. Those for whom I ask are: Gaius Valerius Astraeus, Gaius Valerius Dionysius, Gaius Valerius Aper.
105.1. Since you wish that those who have been deposited with your good faith by Valerius Paulinus should be most honourably provided for, in good time, through me, I have ordered it to be entered in my records that I have for the present given the rights of Roman citizens to those for whom you have now asked—and I will do the same for the rest, for whom you shall ask.
106.1. Being asked, my lord, by Publius Accius Aquila, a centurion of the sixth mounted cohort, to send you a memorial through which he implores your indulgence concerning the status of his daughter, I thought it harsh to refuse, since I knew how much patience and humanity you are accustomed to show to the entreaties of soldiers.
107.1. I have read the memorial of Publius Accius Aquila, centurion of the sixth mounted cohort, which you sent me; and, moved by his entreaties, I have given his daughter Roman citizenship. I have sent you the memorial with my reply, which you are to deliver to him.
108.1. What right you wish both the Bithynian and the Pontic communities to have in exacting the moneys owed to them, whether from leases or sales or other causes, I ask, my lord, that you write back. I have found that by very many proconsuls priority of payment was granted to them, and that it has had the force of law.
108.2. I think, however, that by your foresight something ought to be established and sanctioned by which their interests may be provided for in perpetuity. For the things established by those proconsuls, granted though they were wisely, are yet brief and weak, unless your authority attends them.
109.1. What right the Bithynian or Pontic communities ought to use in those moneys which from whatever cause are owed to the commonwealth, must be determined by the law of each. For, if they have a privilege by which they are preferred to other creditors, it must be observed; if they have not, it will not be right for it to be granted by me to the injury of private persons.

title: Letters
text:
110.1. The advocate of the city of the Amiseni, my lord, claimed before me from Julius Piso about forty thousand denarii given to him publicly, twenty years ago, with the consent of the council and the assembly, and made use of your instructions, by which donations of this kind are forbidden.
110.2. Piso, on the contrary, said that he had contributed very much to the commonwealth and had spent nearly all his resources. He added also the lapse of time, and demanded that he be not compelled to repay, with the overthrow of the rest of his standing, what he had received long ago and on behalf of many services. For which reasons I thought the whole cognizance ought to be deferred, so that I might consult you, my lord, what you think ought to be followed.
111.1. Just as my instructions forbid largesses to be made out of public funds, so, lest the security of many be undermined, things done some time ago ought not to be raked up and annulled. Whatever, therefore, was done on this account more than twenty years ago, let us pass over. For I wish the men of each place to be provided for no less than the public money.
112.1. The Pompeian law, my lord, which the Bithynians and Pontians use, does not order those who are enrolled in the council by the censors to give money; but those whom your indulgence has permitted to be added to certain communities above the lawful number have paid in single and double thousands of denarii.
112.2. Anicius Maximus the proconsul afterwards ordered that even those who were enrolled by the censors should pay in—but only in very few communities, and different sums for different places.
112.3. It remains, therefore, for you yourself to consider whether in all communities all who shall hereafter be enrolled as councillors ought to give a fixed sum for their admission. For that which is to remain in perpetuity should be established by you, to whose deeds and words eternity is owed.
113.1. Whether all who become decurions in each community of Bithynia ought to pay an honorarium for the decurionate or not, cannot be laid down by me in general terms. I think, therefore—what is always safest—that the law of each community should be followed; but more truly I judge that those who are made decurions by invitation will act so as to be preferred to the rest by their contribution.
114.1. By the Pompeian law, my lord, the Bithynian communities are permitted to enrol as their citizens whomever they wish, provided it be none of those communities which are in Bithynia. By the same law it is sanctioned for what causes men may be ejected from the senate by the censors.
114.2. Hence certain of the censors have thought I ought to be consulted whether they ought to eject one who was of another community.
114.3. Since the law, just as it forbade a foreign citizen to be enrolled, so did not order one to be ejected from the senate for this cause; and besides, since it was affirmed to me that in every community there are very many councillors from other communities, and that it would come about that many men and many communities would be shaken by that part of the law which had long since fallen into disuse by a kind of common consent—I thought it necessary to consult you as to what you think ought to be observed. The heads of the law I have appended to this letter.
115.1. With reason you hesitated, my dear Secundus, what ought to be written back by you to the censors who consulted you whether those should remain in the senate who are citizens of other communities, though of the same province. For both the authority of the law and the long custom practised against the law could move you in different directions. This moderate course of it has pleased me: that we should change nothing as to the past, but that those should remain who, though enrolled against the law, are citizens of whatever communities, while for the future the Pompeian law should be observed; for if we should wish to maintain its force retroactively as well, many things must necessarily be thrown into confusion.

title: Letters
text:
116.1. Those who assume the gown of manhood, or celebrate marriages, or enter upon a magistracy, or dedicate a public work, are accustomed to invite the whole council and even no small number from the common people, and to give two denarii apiece or one. I ask you to write whether you think this ought to be observed, and to what extent.
116.2. For I myself, as I judge, think that on solemn occasions especially this right of invitation ought to be allowed; yet I fear that those who invite a thousand men, sometimes even more, may seem to exceed the measure and to fall into the appearance of a public distribution (dianomē).
117.1. With reason you fear that the invitation may fall into the appearance of a public distribution, which both exceeds the measure in number and, as it were, gathers men by whole bodies, not individually one by one from acquaintance, to solemn doles. But I chose your prudence for this very purpose, that you yourself should regulate the morals of that province in shaping them, and should establish those things which would be conducive to the lasting tranquillity of that province.
118.1. The athletes, my lord, think that what you have established for the iselastic contests is owed to them straightway from that day on which they are crowned; for it makes no difference, they say, when they are conveyed into their native city, but when they have won the contest, from which they can be conveyed in. I, on the contrary, write 'in the name of the iselastic privilege': and so I strongly doubt of them whether rather that time ought to be regarded at which they made their entry.
118.2. The same men also claim provisions for that contest which has been made iselastic by you, although they won before it was made so. For they say it is consistent that, just as it is not given them for those contests which ceased to be iselastic after they won, so it should be given them for those which have begun to be so.
118.3. Here too I am no little perplexed, lest account should be taken of anyone retroactively, and that should be given which was not owed at the time when they won. I ask, then, that you deign to guide my hesitation—that is, to interpret your own benefits yourself.
119.1. The iselastic privilege seems to me to begin to be owed only from the time when anyone has himself made his entry into his own city. The provisions for those contests which it has pleased me to be iselastic, if they were not iselastic before, are not owed retroactively. Nor can it avail for the athletes' desire that they ceased to receive the rewards of those which, after they won, I have established not to be iselastic. For, the condition of the contests having been changed, the rewards they had received before are nonetheless not recalled.
120.1. Up to this time, my lord, I have lent warrants of post to no one, nor sent them for any business but yours. But a certain necessity has broken this constant observance of mine.
120.2. For when my wife had heard of the death of her grandfather and wished to hasten to her aunt, I thought it harsh to deny her the use of them, since the grace of such a duty rests on speed, and I knew that you would approve the cause of her journey, which was family affection. This I have written to you because I seemed to myself too little grateful if I concealed that, among other benefits, I owed this one too to your indulgence—that, in the confidence of it, I did not hesitate to do, as though by consulting you, a thing which, had I consulted you, I should have done too late.

title: Letters
text: 121.1. With reason you had confidence in my disposition, my dear Secundus; nor would there have been any need to hesitate, if you had waited until you consulted me, whether your wife's journey ought to be assisted by the warrants of post which I gave for your office, since your wife ought to add even by speed to the grace of her arrival at her aunt's.
